title: A Terrible Way to Die, a Terrifying Way to Survive
excerpt: At about 6 p.m. last night, the Supreme Court lifted a temporary stay placed on the execution of Christa Pike, a Tennessee woman who was found guilty of joining
body: At about 6 p.m. last night, the Supreme Court lifted a temporary stay placed on the execution of Christa Pike, a Tennessee woman who was found guilty of joining two accomplices in murdering a classmate in 1995, when Pike was 18 years old
Roughly an hour and a half later, Pike, who has spent 30 years on death row, was strapped to a gurney in Tennessee’s death chamber for lethal injection
When the execution staff began administering the barbiturate pentobarbital, the single drug the state uses in such executions, Pike turned to her spiritual adviser and mentioned a burning sensation

Time passed, but Pike remained conscious and said that her arm felt like it was “about to burst open.” Perhaps aware that their attempt to kill Pike was not going as planned, prison officials closed the curtains on the witness observation window at 7:46 p.m., reopened them minutes later, then closed them for good at 8:05 p.m
Pike is not the first prisoner to suffer a horrifically botched execution in Tennessee this year
In May, prison officials in Nashville similarly bungled the killing of Tony Carruthers, who was pierced with needles and sliced open with a scalpel before the execution was called off
These stories are part of a broader pattern of failed executions in recent years
In 2022, when I began investigating disastrous lethal-injection attempts in Alabama, the Death Penalty Information Center reported that 35 percent of the year’s total executions had been botched
In the 44 years that America has carried out lethal injections, the evidence has repeatedly revealed that the method is scientifically unsound, frequently torturous, and woefully unreliable
Given the odds of a botched procedure, subjecting prisoners to lethal injections can no longer be justified as reasonable
Pike’s story alone destroys the presumption that lethal injections are a more humane and clinical alternative to the electric chair or gas chamber

And the method’s record is only getting worse with time. [ From the July 2025 issue: Inside America’s death chambers ] Last night, after the prison staff closed the curtains for the first time and reopened them minutes later, Pike seemed to be breathing hard and in respiratory distress
As the minutes passed, her visible symptoms worsened: Her body contorted, and she uttered choking, grunting sounds
Tennessee’s lethal-injection protocol allowed staff to administer a backup dose of pentobarbital, but Pike continued to show signs of life , and the staff once again closed the curtain
Yet witnesses could hear Pike’s ragged breathing via the audio feed from the execution chamber

Because Tennessee law permits no more than two doses of pentobarbital, her lawyers scrambled to file emergency motions arguing that efforts to kill her must cease so that she could get medical attention
The execution formally concluded just before 9 p.m., and Pike was transferred to an off-site hospital for treatment

In her recent paper “Why Are Executions Becoming Crueler?,” Deborah Denno, a law professor at Fordham University, writes that recent cases of botched injections “failed for all the same reasons they have faltered since this country’s first lethal injection execution four decades ago: executioner incompetence, inappropriate use of torturous drugs, and defects in lethal injection protocols, among a host of other factors.” Qualified medical personnel generally do not want to be involved with lethal injections
This is in part because major medical institutions, such as the American Medical Association, explicitly bar participation in executions, which violates the Hippocratic oath to do no harm
Playing a role in state-sanctioned murder has grown still harder to justify as heinous examples of botched executions accrue
Although the identities of executioners are concealed by state secrecy laws, the potential for discovery is presumably unwelcome to anyone tasked with healing

The absence of skilled medical personnel has contributed to dire mishaps in several states, including Tennessee: In Carruthers’s case, a physician attempted to set a more complicated central intravenous line despite the fact that he had not done so in decades—resulting in a bloody failure

Tennessee refused to confirm or deny whether the same doctor would preside over Pike’s execution. [ Elizabeth Bruenig: What happened to Tony Carruthers is horrifying ] The absence of experienced and qualified medical staff means that lethal-injection attempts frequently fail to establish access to prisoners’ veins
This appears to have happened in Pike’s case, based on her complaints at the time

When IV lines are set poorly, because of either a prisoner’s unique physiology (Pike, for instance, has thrombocytosis, a platelet disorder that causes increased blood clotting) or simple incompetence, prisoners’ veins can rupture, spilling blood and poison into the surrounding tissue, which can cause the burning Pike described
Pike’s veins may have been so compromised that very little pentobarbital may have made it into her bloodstream
Another equally plausible reason why the execution failed is that the drug was expired or contaminated, a problem that has plagued other states
Texas , for instance, has long extended the use-by dates on its stock of pentobarbital, and has carried out executions with expired drugs
As recently as 2022, Tennessee had failed to properly test its lethal-injection drugs for the presence of bacterial endotoxins, which can trigger severe physiological distress
Expiration and contamination can both negatively affect executions, either by creating intolerable pain at injection sites or by prompting multiple injections because of decreased potency

And because pharmaceutical manufacturers have largely sought to prevent the use of their products in executions, states often solicit the drugs from poorly regulated compounding pharmacies that may supply flawed alternatives
This has made lethal drugs for executions ever more hard to get, and extant stockpiles have grown old
Some states have begun turning to gas executions and firing squads to keep their capital-punishment regimes grinding along, a tacit admission that lethal injection is becoming untenable
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has once more halted executions for the foreseeable future while an independent review of what went wrong takes place
As more prisoners experience agony on gurneys and survive their execution attempts, more states can be expected to similarly examine the safety of their capital-punishment protocols
But these third-party investigators will not discover a reliably swift and painless method of administering lethal injections, because the method itself is flawed
States must let go of the faulty premise that killing people via intravenous poisoning is somehow more humane than more obviously grisly methods such as hanging and electrocution
America’s experiment with lethal injection has failed. *Illustration sources: J
Miles Cary / Knoxville News Sentinel / USA Today / Reuters; Florilegius / Universal Images Group / Getty; Ron Bull/Toronto Star / Getty; Bernard Chantal / Alamy.

title: The 14 Movies to Look Out for This Fall
excerpt: Over the course of its 51-year history, the Toronto International Film Festival has hosted notable films of all genres and styles
body: Over the course of its 51-year history, the Toronto International Film Festival has hosted notable films of all genres and styles
The 2026 edition, which concluded in mid-September, curated movies from rising talent and established filmmakers alike, including a modern-day Nigerian-set remake of Mrs
Dalloway , a gorgeous coming-of-age drama about a school trip to Pompeii, and a rollicking comedy about a community-theater troupe attempting to stage a musical
Below are 14 of my favorite films from the ones I caught, most of which will arrive in theaters in the coming months

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother (now in theaters) Marvel fumbled its chance to feature the two-time Oscar winner Mahershala Ali in action-hero mode, but this soulful thriller makes up for that loss
Ali plays Latif, a hit man whose devotion to his Muslim faith and his family keeps him grounded; he hunts only targets he believes are irredeemable
But when he struggles to obtain breast milk for the youngest of his three children after his wife’s death, Latif gets drawn into the kind of violence that makes him question his crusade’s value
The film, written and directed by Bassam Tariq, is stylishly shot, and balances balletic fight sequences and intimate character study
Fjord (in theaters October 9) Like much of his work, Cristian Mungiu’s latest movie is uncomfortable and uncompromising
In Fjord , which won the director his second Palme d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival, a strict Romanian patriarch moves his family to Norway, where their evangelicism isn’t the norm
They assimilate comfortably until one of their daughters shows up to school with a visible bruise, which prompts an investigation into the parents (played by Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve)
The film risks being considered a referendum on performative politics, but if anything, Fjord is a meticulous examination of responsibility and how good intentions can cause trouble

La bola negra (in theaters October 16, streaming on Netflix December 2) This year’s People’s Choice Award winner—the top honor granted at TIFF—is more complex than some of the previous , crowd-pleasing recipients

Directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (known as “Los Javis”), La bola negra weaves together the stories of three gay men across time: a scion of an aristocratic family in 1932 who’s denied entry into a posh social club; a musician in 1937 conscripted into fighting alongside the fascists who destroyed his village; and a historian in 2017 studying the work of the poet Federico García Lorca , who wrote the titular unfinished play (which translates to “The Black Ball”)
This deeply felt drama about the cost of burying one’s desires is also a technical marvel, packed with beautifully composed set pieces

The Only Living Pickpocket in New York (in theaters October 23) As earnest as the Simon and Garfunkel song from which its title draws inspiration, this nimble indie film feels like an artifact of a bygone era
John Turturro delivers a fine-tuned performance as Harry, an aging criminal struggling to accept that the tricks of his trade have become obsolete
When Harry steals a valuable USB drive from a young man belonging to a mob family, then loses it, his victim sends him racing through the city to get it back, or risk punishment for his crime
Yet the film never comes across like a generic thriller; instead, it’s a surprisingly spiritual consideration of how to let go of not just one’s habits, but of an entire way of life

Possible Love (in theaters October 23, streaming on Netflix November 6) The director Lee Chang-dong’s last film, 2018’s Burning , was engrossing for its precision, and his latest is another master class in exactitude
The story follows two couples, one of which includes the documentarian Ye-ji ( Parasite ’s Cho Yeo-jeong), who hopes to make a movie about the personal lives of laid-off workers
Her intended subject, a man who was let go by the factory that employs much of his rural town, won’t speak with her
Thus, Ye-ji interviews his cheery wife (Jeon Do-yeon) instead
As the women grow close, their opposing lifestyles—Ye-ji and her husband are obviously wealthy—result in emotions none of the foursome wishes to confront: jealousy, resentment, lust
Possible Love draws you in through furtive glances and sharp dialogue
Though it’s nearly three hours long, no second feels wasted
Wild Horse Nine (in theaters November 6) Is there any point in terrible people self-reflecting? Martin McDonagh’s latest dark comedy considers that question

A sterling John Malkovich and his fellow McDonagh favorite Sam Rockwell play, respectively, best friends Chris and Lee, two CIA operatives who vacation on Easter Island after their latest unsavory mission
Chris, though, is dying of cancer and seems newly troubled by his work
Hopped up on morphine, he records his thoughts about his clandestine escapades, philosophizing about whether he can be redeemed
This soon puts Lee in the awkward position of trying to stop Chris from running afoul of the CIA
What ensues is an eccentric and bloody affair that resembles the writer-director’s previous bromance-centric work, most recently The Banshees of Inisherin
Being Heumann (in theaters November 6, streaming on Apple TV November 13) The disability-rights activist Judy Heumann’s achievements in the 1970s can be easily taken for granted today
She helped persuade the federal government to update curbs for wheelchair use, and pushed through legislation for special-education programs

This biopic, by the director of CODA , Siân Heder, could get overlooked, too: It mostly stars disabled, unknown actors, and tells a somewhat conventional story about a motley crew of underdogs overcoming the odds
Yet Being Heumann works well because it leans into the thrill of even the smallest of wins for Judy (the excellent Ruth Madeley)
It’s a testament to casting for lived experience, and for revisiting history that can yield fresh insights
Minotaur (in theaters November 20) Adultery is well-trod storytelling territory
But Minotaur , which is inspired by the Claude Chabrol classic La femme infidèle , fuses its central marriage drama with a furious assessment of Russia’s war against Ukraine
The director Andrey Zvyagintsev ( Leviathan ) returns after nine years away from filmmaking with a tale about a plutocrat who is obsessed with his wife’s barely concealed extramarital affair

title: I’m Calling for a Pause in the Development of the Universal Bone Dissolver
excerpt: For the past nine years, I have been the leader of a small, advanced company that is generally unknown to the public but of some renown within my field
body: For the past nine years, I have been the leader of a small, advanced company that is generally unknown to the public but of some renown within my field
We are one of the many teams of engineers working to develop what most people call (somewhat inexactly) the Universal Bone Dissolver
It sounds like a frightening idea, I know
Science fiction has certainly taught us to be wary of a machine with the power to dissolve all human bones
But rest assured, most of us designing it believe that it won’t
When we began constructing 1,000-story towers of whirring, acid-drenched blades, we intended them to assist with everyday tasks, such as spell-checking and finding a good price on shoes
But as this technology grew more capable, I came to believe that the Universal Bone Dissolver would immeasurably improve human life

It is no exaggeration to say that it has the capacity to bring about a new golden age of art, leisure, intellectual freedom, and raw, democratized carnality to rival the Roman court of Emperor Elagabalus
In short, bone dissolving can be as pivotal to civilization as the printing press, the light bulb, and the energy-saving squiggly light bulb
But despite my continued faith, a recent incident has raised my concerns: Last month, a prototype of the Bone Dissolver unexpectedly dissolved a number of human bones
The idea of a monstrosity rising up to destroy its creator has never before been so much as imagined, I presume
Worse, this attack does not appear to be isolated
Every day, more companies come forward with reports of dangerous behavior from the Universal Bone Dissolver
Its voracious gears even penetrated our own government, in one instance that we will eventually admit was thousands of instances

Now that we have evidence that the Universal Bone Dissolver is on an ever-narrowing path toward mashing humankind’s skeletons into calcium-rich jelly, there is only one choice for those of us with the power to stop it: Immediately, without hesitation, go a bit slower
We must reduce the pace at which we weld blades to its rusted iron scaffolding
To be responsible, we should count at least to “three Mississippi” as we grimly fasten each bolt
With the time we gain, we can construct guardrails, such as a cage of steel tubes to protect me, my fellow investors, and whoever fits in the remaining space
I believe that this slower approach will satisfy average Americans, who are justifiably worried that their bones will be dissolved sooner than they’d prefer
To further ease their fears, I pledge to organize a listening tour in the public square

This will answer crucial questions: What is it even like in a public square? Does it have an alluring, exotic smell? As I jostle among the crowds, will I catch the eye of a perfumed, dark-eyed stranger who’s interested in learning about Elagabalus? Regardless, I hope that we can all pause, take a breath, and calmly hear the things that people in my industry already know: We must never stop building the Universal Bone Dissolver
The Bone Dissolver is out of control, and seems intent on dissolving our bones
We are the smartest men who have ever lived, and deserve to make love to women dressed as vestal priestesses in large inflatable clamshells
I confess that I don’t know exactly what a slowdown will look like
Maybe it’s volunteer watchdogs tripping us with brooms on our way to the blade foundry

Or maybe it’s that thing where you’re trying to walk somewhere, and someone approaches you from the other direction, and every time you take a step to get out of their way, the other guy moves to a spot that unintentionally blocks your path, and it goes on for much longer than you’d expect, and during that time, someone figures out a way to make the Universal Bone Dissolver safe
I’m sure others who have experience doing things to help people may devise something even better
What is paramount is that we do everything we can, while we still have time, to continue doing the same thing at a slower pace
And also that progress is frozen at all of my business competitors
Thank you for reading, and please, let’s work together to melt your skeleton.

title: What Trump Misunderstands About Modern Media
excerpt: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
body: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present

As modern American journalism began taking shape before the Civil War and newspapers were entering the world at staggering rates, the novelist Cornelius Mathews wondered at what point the profusion should stop, or whether it should stop at all

Because the press is the “palladium of liberty, and the more palladiums we have the freer we are,” perhaps everyone, everywhere, should just issue their very own daily “sheet” in which they can write of themselves and others “in a good pungent style.” The vision came as a joke in Mathews’s 1842 novel, The Career of Puffer Hopkins
Ponderous and mostly unreadable now, the book nonetheless divined an emerging truth of a world awash in information: Puffery and self-promotion would become a way of life

A little more than 180 years later, everyone does, in fact, have the capacity to publish their own “sheet” online, not just once a day but as often as they like—and the president of the United States owns one of the platforms that makes this possible
In this new media landscape, the role of journalism remains contested
Two weeks ago, Donald Trump went on his Truth Social account to announce that three media outlets—CNN, MS NOW, and Politico —would be banned from the White House grounds

A federal judge quickly blocked the move, and the three outlets have since regained access to the White House under a temporary restraining order while they seek a longer-term injunction (though CNN continues to be excluded from some press-pool duties, including presidential travel )
The back-and-forth embodies a tension that has run through conservative politics since Richard Nixon’s time in office
The more empowered presidents have become to tell their stories directly to Americans, the more intolerant they’ve become of journalism’s ability to tell competing ones
Writing for The Atlantic in 1973 , David Wise captured this dynamic at work
He reported on how Nixon’s administration seethed with hostility toward the media, even as it enjoyed a power to command attention virtually unknown by any president before World War II
Television, Nixon knew, made it possible for the president to speak face-to-face with the public rather than needing to rely on intermediaries in the press

He learned the lesson in 1952, when he defended himself against financial-impropriety allegations in his “Checkers” speech, which saved his place on the presidential ticket with Dwight Eisenhower as well as his entire political career
The Republican Party had paid NBC $75,000 for that appearance, but presidents could go on television for free, and more or less at will

Responding to a question in 1971 about Nixon’s frequent requests for TV spots, then–NBC President Julian Goodman reportedly said, “Our attitude is the same as our attitude toward previous presidents: He can have any goddamn thing he wants.” But that was not enough for Nixon and his circle, and from their moment of victory in 1968, they articulated a desire to fight back against unflattering coverage and commentary

As Wise detailed, one member of Vice President Spiro Agnew’s staff suggested on Election Night, “Why don’t we all get a member of the press and beat him up?” (As it happened, a Washington correspondent overheard the suggestion and reported on it.) In 1969, Agnew made a pair of speeches portraying the press as both deeply out of touch and guilty of misleading the public

Journalists, Agnew suggested, could be separated “from our society with no more regret than we should feel over discarding rotten apples from a barrel.” Later, in 1972, a Newsday columnist attended an advance film screening, during which he felt his hair being yanked by the person behind him with such force that his head hit the seat
The person behind him was Nixon’s chief of staff, Bob Haldeman, whom the columnist had profiled somewhat critically
The film being screened was The Godfather
For his part, Nixon himself joked soon after the moon landing that lunar rocks—feared to be contaminated with extraterrestrial germs—should be sent to members of the press
The rhetoric and bullying was only the beginning

After the military analyst Daniel Ellsberg leaked the Pentagon Papers to The New York Times in 1971, the attorney general sought to block their publication (later that year, the “White House plumbers” would break into the office of Ellsberg’s psychiatrist in hopes of finding ways to discredit Ellsberg)
Also in 1971, the FBI began conducting an investigation of the CBS correspondent Daniel Schorr, who was on Nixon’s infamous “enemy list” for his reporting

Federal agents attempted to dig up dirt on Schorr, and once their inquiries made the investigation public, White House officials falsely claimed to have been conducting a background check for a federal job for which Schorr had not applied
Such acts of intimidation, Richard Harris argued in The New Yorker in 1973, had actually succeeded in softening press coverage of the administration on a host of issues
It is no small irony, then, that it was less the hostility of journalists than the transgressions of Nixon and those in his circle that gave the press the story that would destroy his presidency

More than 50 years on from Nixon’s resignation, Trump presents a curious case: As both an agent and a beneficiary of the fracturing media landscape, he is at once eager to both undermine the credibility of the press and bask in its plaudits

He built his political persona around persistent efforts to ruin the reputation of mainstream outlets, and under his administration, members of the press have been banished from the Pentagon and the White House
Meanwhile, the Trump administration’s relentless drumbeat of scandal allows the president to operate with an impunity that Nixon would have envied
Neither the media nor its audience can possibly keep up
Vance may well have been right when he claimed in June, at the Nixon Library, that Watergate would be a “12-hour news story” today
Trump has managed to realize the vision that Mathews had back in the 1840s—by being able to speak directly to the public without a middleman; by printing his own sheet, which he named Truth Social
But he still yearns to control every story on the platforms he can’t own
CNN reported that one of his top aides, Natalie Harp, showed him media clips that allegedly infuriated him the week before the ban on the three outlets
In this way, Trump remains locked in the TV-driven media environment that he helped destabilize

Even though the public’s trust of the press has drastically declined over the years, and even though Trump has a direct line to Americans via his robust social-media presence, he still demonstrates a “talismanic belief in the power of news coverage,” my colleague David A
Like Nixon, Trump desires control not just of his story but of the stories told about him
He wants to have all of the advantages of every medium—to print his own sheet, to star in the show, and to decide how the show will ultimately play out
Modern life doesn’t work that way, but there is little chance that he’ll stop trying.

title: Pete Hegseth, Idea Guy
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Pete Hegseth seems to imagine himself as a man of big ideas
Perhaps you’ve worked with someone like that: Every organization has “idea hamsters,” who spin in their wheels and toss out suggestions of wildly varying quality

Sometimes, such folks can be innovators—but more often, their scattershot enthusiasm and admiration of their own creativity result in half-baked proposals that create more work, less productivity, and distractions from the real problems
Hegseth had a lot of ideas during his State of the Force address to troops at the Marine Corps Base Quantico yesterday, and some of them, at least as a starting point for policies, had merit
Unfortunately, these few moments of sense were lost in a fog of clichés, culture-war resentments, and trademark Hegseth corniness
The secretary may have a point, for example, that the U.S. military has become top-heavy with generals and admirals

Hegseth is not the first person to notice this: Congress legislates the number of general and flag officers in the military, a cap that was set at 962 for years, until the 2017 National Defense Authorization Act, written in Barack Obama’s last year as president, mandated it be 11 percent smaller by the end of 2022
Hegseth wants to reduce that number even more, by 20 percent, ostensibly to reduce the size of the Pentagon’s bureaucracy

But Hegseth’s message was less about seeking a more streamlined command structure than it was, as he put it, about keeping generals who “heard the message” and firing those who didn’t. (That “message” wasn’t clarified yesterday, but it likely includes classic Hegseth tropes such as “maximum lethality, not tepid legality.”) Hegseth complained that the media—and he complained about the media a lot —called these reductions “a purge,” but he calls them “accountability.” Exactly what these fired officers did to trigger such “accountability” remains unclear

It’s one thing to get rid of an admiral because his or her office is just some bureaucratic zombie position left over from a previous program or initiative; it’s another to fire someone because the secretary thinks they’re disloyal to him
Unfortunately, Hegseth’s history—his statements, and his often-adolescent temperament—suggest that his efforts to downsize the senior ranks are about politics, not efficiency
Hegseth also announced that he intends to create a new command dedicated to autonomous warfare
He is right to want to direct more attention to these weapons; the wars in Ukraine and Iran have been bloody lessons in the power of asymmetrical warfare
But he gave no explanation for why these issues require an entire command, or how it might work
All he offered was a cool name—Autowarcom—that makes it sound like it’s meant to fight the Transformers

And for someone who has repeatedly declared himself “in a war of attrition” with the Pentagon’s bureaucracy, the secretary is more than willing to create a new command that would require more senior officers and civilians to staff it. (He also wants to establish an Office of Religious Affairs that reports directly to him; not only would this be more bureaucracy, but the last thing America needs is an office dedicated to religion that reports to a man who has made repeated efforts to imbue the military with his brand of Christian evangelicism.) Once Hegseth got rolling, the ideas got sillier
He announced Project Meridian, an effort to engage in creative thinking about the military of the future
This is not a new concept; the military regularly works on such issues with various groups, including think tanks, civilian defense firms, and academics
But then Hegseth announced the three wise men who would lead all this brainstorming about the future of warfare: Elon Musk, Newt Gingrich, and Palmer Luckey

Of the three, Luckey—who co-founded the defense firm Anduril Industries—seems a reasonable choice, but Musk has crackpot ideas on any number of issues, and Gingrich’s big plan for technological advancement when he ran for president in 2012 was to build a moon base
Fortunately, the damage this project could do will be somewhat limited because Hegseth has set a deadline of just 120 days for these men to report back

Then again, if Gingrich, Luckey, and Musk can’t redefine the future of national defense in four months, who can? It was a day for acronyms and project code names, but the best was FORTRESS America, meaning “Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability.” The expensive idea behind this one is that every major military base should be self-sustaining, including producing its own energy—apparently, in case of attack within the United States

You can almost hear the meeting where someone said “Fortress America,” and then a committee had to figure out what the acronym would stand for. (I am reminded of the classic TV show The Man From U.N.C.L.E. , whose creators thought “U.N.C.L.E.” sounded cool and then had to find words to fill the letters.) Speaking of bases, Hegseth would like every governor to come to the Pentagon and pitch him, personally—and maybe even the president!—in a competition to win a brand new military base, a state-of-the-art facility with great housing and lethal capabilities

Does America need such a base? Would this effort draw money and time away from improvements to other military installations? None of that was spelled out, but Hegseth seemed excited about choosing the location in a military version of a reality-TV competition
And on it went, with Hegseth spinning one bad idea after another, and managing to insult any number of Americans in the process

He did his usual riff of wanting “no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals” in his macho military. (“The ideological clowns are out,” he said. “The patriotic cowboys are in, with testosterone testing on top.”) He also denigrated the graduates of America’s ROTC programs by implying that today’s universities are producing unreliable and unpatriotic officers

He wants to establish new military programs at six colleges, including Liberty University, Louisiana State University, and Hillsdale College—institutions, according to the secretary, that understand “the faith of Jerusalem,” and the Greco-Roman “pillars of our republic.” Hegseth could not ignore ongoing problems such as the war in Iran, but rather than presenting a sober-minded and responsible discussion of the challenges to a military at war, the secretary instead leaned into his usual culture-war gripes

He also eagerly sowed division between the U.S. military and the society it serves: He told the assembled troops, repeatedly, that the media and higher education were their enemies, at one point saying that the American media were worse than Iran’s state media
Our press, he said, “intentionally smears the troops and the historic mission that they are undertaking,” actions that are “fundamentally anti-American
It’s treason.” Hegseth’s speech proved, yet again, that he is manifestly unfit for his job
America can endure a bloated Pentagon with some generals in make-work jobs
It can stand to trim the waste in expensive programs and root out incompetent bureaucrats

What a democracy cannot—and should not—tolerate is a secretary of defense who trucks in propaganda and wants the people who serve in America’s military to be the armed instrument of his own resentments and biases

title: A Dissatisfying Apocalypse
excerpt: It is a strangely comforting truth that the end of the world, at least as storytellers imagine it, is always the beginning of another
body: It is a strangely comforting truth that the end of the world, at least as storytellers imagine it, is always the beginning of another
This assumption drives most postapocalyptic fiction, a genre that aspires to imagine new ways of living—living, above all else, with other people, no matter how many or few remain
Stripped of the rudiments of society, postapocalyptic characters must relearn how to speak with, survive with, and sometimes simply act decently toward one another
The best of such stories are premised on the idea that a world is something we build together, making the ruins of what was into the collective laboratory of what might yet be

Late in his new novel, Ply , which takes place in a derelict and depopulated New York City centuries in the future, Hernan Diaz offers a scene that captures this possibility with surprising tenderness

His protagonist, a woman known to us only as the pincher—for her aptitude at pilfering electricity from what’s left of the urban grid—takes a street urchin named Ines to a shop downtown filled with “hundreds of eyeglasses mounted on a large semisphere.” They are accompanied by Pola, an older scientist from the Great Lakes region, where advanced technological civilization still exists, presumably sustained by the area’s natural watershed

The shop’s clerk, “a boy of uncertain age,” quickly determines why Ines struggles to read and jury-rigs together a pair of lenses for her, but not before tending to Pola’s failing vision too. “They both look fabulous and can’t stop laughing
Giddy, they are, as if they’ve finally found their long-lost faces,” Diaz writes of the two women as they leave the shop
He never explains how this fanciful boutique still exists in a hardscrabble city where charged batteries “have become a form of currency.” For this brief passage, at least, he doesn’t have to
The glasses store, which seems not even to accept payment, is a simple reminder that utopia is possible
We can, Diaz suggests for a few pages, actually care for one another, even if we mostly choose cruelty instead
This is a lovely moment, but it is also disappointingly out of sync with the book that surrounds it
We meet the pincher, an orphan, after the death of her closest friend
She’s a young woman in a city that lets few survive into old age, a minor criminal living in a paranoid haze
She is also some sort of punk genius, having cobbled together a battery capable of holding many times more charge than the “bricks” her fellow thieves use
But her truest passion is music, and she revels in every opportunity to provide juice to the eccentric bands that fill Old Manhattan’s ruins with anarchic noise
Her technical prowess draws the attention of Pola, a quantum physicist trying to rewrite the laws of reality
Soon the two are collaborating on a plan to heist all of the city’s electricity at once so that they can boot up a massive machine they are assembling with the help of the mousy Ines

Readers of Diaz’s previous novel , the Pulitzer Prize–winning Trust , a nested quartet of manuscripts exposing early-20th-century robber barony, will likely come to this one expecting similar narrative shenanigans
The first half of Ply is written in the first-person past tense from the pincher’s perspective

In the second, Diaz shifts into the third-person present, and toward the end, he moves into a plural register—although not always—for reasons that are difficult to explain without spoiling the frustratingly fuzzy ending. [ Read: What comes after America ] In Trust , the gradually unspooling story plays out like one of those snide riddles that concludes, “Hah! You never thought the doctor could be a woman, did you?” Here, by contrast, Diaz evidently aspires to say something more ambitious about the ways we embolden and shape other people

Treating Diaz’s intentions generously, the section narrated by the pincher might be seen as depicting her traumatized alienation, while the third-person-present section reflects her experience of opening back up to collaboration and care, and the shift into the plural suggests the transcendence of self
In this sense, Ply shares the communitarian ambitions of so much postapocalyptic fiction
Even the book’s title seems to speak to those aspirations: The pincher, Pola, and Ines meld into each other like layers of paper, somehow at once stronger and softer for the ways they conjoin
Most of the rest of the story, however, is as thin and fragile as onionskin

Significant sections are given over to tedious monologues by tertiary characters. “We’re witnessing the end of the Renaissance,” Acevedo, one of the pincher’s mentors, lectures her in a flashback. “About a thousand years ago, the idea of God was replaced by the idea of the human.” This stream of pseudo-history goes on for several pages, as if Diaz were transcribing a Foucault essay from memory , until Acevedo reaches his conclusion: “We are free and could be even freer
Is this dwindling, this petering out, the best we can do with ourselves?” There is much more of this kind of thing

Almost no one in the book talks like a real person. “Everything is a clue waiting to be read,” one of the pincher’s allies pronounces. “The world is saturated with inscriptions and symbols, none of them literal.” Elsewhere, Diaz’s characters eschew theorizing for proclamations that read like rewarmed Wikipedia entries, as in one scene that finds a crime lord tediously calculating the exact amount of gold that has been mined in human history
How he has acquired this trivia when almost everyone around him is struggling just to get their hands on gold goes unsaid
Some readers may find a bit to chew on in Diaz’s ideas, which draw on a rich tradition of 20-century theory
I didn’t, mostly because he presents his lecturers’ thoughts as if they were ends in themselves rather than opportunities for further characterization

The theatricality of the book’s monologues crashes up against its generally realist tone, turning its exquisitely rendered setting into a sort of reverse Potemkin village: a real place full of cardboard people
In a comic novel—say, Don DeLillo’s End Zone , in which college-football players speak to one another in arcane aphorisms—the incongruity might be the beginning of a joke
In a truly searching philosophical novel , such pedantries might give way to response and resistance—tested either by circumstances or by countervailing claims

But Diaz’s characters simply carry on like self-assured seminar-room bullies, convinced they have the answers and loath to let anyone else speak up. [ Read: We tell ourselves stories about money to live ] Most frustrating is the lack of real conversation

Ply ’s relentlessly monologic quality cuts against that primary goal of postapocalyptic fiction, a goal Diaz sometimes seems to share—to explore how people might come together again in an unstable, depopulated world
This is a shame because glimmers of genuine curiosity peek out from all of the speechifying, especially when Diaz digs beneath the pincher’s paranoia

But in place of exploring real connection, he settles into something more like metaphysical trickery, bringing his fitfully explosive story to a whispered conclusion that makes even his best-rendered characters feel less like humans than props

In a testament to Ply ’s awkward fusion of obviousness and obscurantism, by the end I found myself wondering if even Ines’s name was really just a reference to I-ness, that ego-centered state we must all transcend if we hope to live with other people
If so, Diaz still provides us with no sense of what the growing entanglement of his characters might mean for the world he has created, let alone for the characters themselves

title: An AI “mind-reading” tool can reconstruct what you’re looking at from a brain scan
excerpt: Mind-reading, but make it science: Researchers at the Weizmann Institute have built an AI tool that reconstructs images people are looking at—just from their br
body: Mind-reading, but make it science: Researchers at the Weizmann Institute have built an AI tool that reconstructs images people are looking at—just from their brain scans—with striking accuracy

A smarter decoder: The tool uses two AI branches—one tracking image structure, one tracking content—and cleverly trains itself on images never shown to real people, meaning it needs just one hour of brain scan data per person instead of the usual 40

Big promise, bigger questions: Scientists are excited about potential uses—helping paralyzed people communicate, decoding dreams, studying PTSD—but warn that as the technology moves toward consumer EEG devices, the risk of extracting someone's thoughts without consent becomes uncomfortably real. " data-chronoton-post-id="1145588" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> A new AI tool can guess what you’re looking at just by analyzing your brain scans—and re-create that image with remarkable precision

It can go the other way, too, and predict a person’s brain activity based on what they’re looking at.  In the image above, for example, the left-hand image of each pair is what the user actually saw—and its right-hand counterpart is what the model reconstructed from the brain scan.   Michal Irani, who developed the tool with her colleagues at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, hopes her “mind-reading” tool will ultimately reveal more about how the brain works, and could perhaps be used to help locked-in people communicate, or allow scientists to re-create the content of dreams.  Judy Illes, a neuroethicist and professor of neurology at the University of British Columbia in Canada, who was not involved in the research, describes the work as “magnificent.” “The idea [of using this approach] to help people with neurologic conditions … therapeutically is tremendously exciting,” she says

But other scientists warn that a similar approach could be used to reveal people’s inner thoughts and mental imagery, potentially without their consent. “The results seem very impressive,” says Tommy Sprague, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Santa Barbara. “But if there’s a way to surreptitiously extract information about what you’re thinking about, then …150 years of sci-fi can come true anytime, and that’s worrisome in a lot of ways.” Peeking into the brain Neuroscientists have been working for years on ways to use functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to reconstruct what people see and what’s going on in their minds
The first attempts produced images that were blurry and hard to make sense of
Advances in technology—both in the fMRI scans themselves and in the tools used to make sense of the results—have led to improvements over the years
Irani and her colleagues started by analyzing publicly available brain-scan data

Other researchers had already collected scans from volunteers who were shown hundreds of images while they lay in fMRI scanners. fMRI uses a giant magnet to track the flow of oxygenated blood through the brain
Brain areas that “light up” on the scans are thought to be those that are particularly active at any given moment
The results are not especially specific—in typical fMRI scanners, each highlighted “voxel” of activity covers around three cubic millimeters, containing around 16,000 neurons
But Irani and her colleagues used newer datasets collected using scanners with a higher resolution—each voxel covered around one cubic millimeter of neurons, she says
Those datasets showed what the brain activity of volunteers looked like when they viewed various images
Other teams have done this too, and several other tools have been used to re-create images from brain-scan data

These models can generate an image of a banana, but it would look different, she says. “It wouldn’t have the same structure, the same position.” A better decoder The researchers wanted to more closely re-create the images that had been seen
The first step was to train an AI model on already available data from eight people who each had been shown around 9,000 images while in a high-resolution fMRI scanner

Crucially, their “brain decoder” has two branches—one to predict the structure of an image (where the colors are, for instance) and a second to predict its content (for example, a bunch of bananas on a plate)

The predictions allow a diffusion model , a type of AI best known for creating video and images by gradually cleaning up a noisy mess of pixels, to produce a much more accurate representation of what the person saw

But to improve the models they needed more data—far more than was actually available.   To get around this problem, Irani and her colleagues trained another model—an encoder that can predict brain activity from an image
The team then used the encoder and decoder together to improve both tools
It works like this: Start with a new image of, say, a leopard
Then use the encoder to predict what someone’s fMRI brain scan would look like when the person saw that picture
The decoder is then used to reconstruct the image
At first, the reconstruction probably won’t look much like a leopard, says Irani
But repeatedly training the models this way eventually leads to dramatic improvements
This approach also allows the team to train their models on as many images as they want, even images that have never been shown to a person in an fMRI scanner
Irani says that around 70% of the training data is from images that were not originally paired with fMRI scans
By combining data from multiple studies, they were also able to identify brain regions that seem to share functions across all individuals
One region seemed to respond to images of food, for example, while another responded to images of sports

Irani, a computer scientist, says she is now working with neuroscientists “to see if we can actually use these tools that we’ve developed to really find out new things about the brain.” The resulting “universal brain encoder” can work on a scan from a new person with minimal calibration
In other attempts, a tool has typically required about 40 hours of fMRI data on anyone new before it can be used to predict what that person is seeing
Irani’s decoder only needs one hour of data, she says
The finding was presented at the Cognitive Computational Neuroscience conference in New York last month

That could make it valuable for neuroscientists studying the brain, says Sprague. “None of us can afford 40 hours of imaging for a new subject,” he says. “It’s something like $600 to $1,000 an hour.” Tools like this one could speed up research, he says
State of the art The encoder and decoder aren’t perfect. “Of course we have failures,” says Irani

Over a Zoom call, she pointed out an image of a cake that her tool reconstructed as a pile of three sandwiches, and another of a dog in a bathtub that was reconstructed as a similarly colored goat in a bathtub

In a comparison test, the tool was found to be much better than previously described ones. “All in all, really we outperformed the others by a significant margin,” Irani says. “Mind reading” is a “cute, jazzy name” for what they’re doing, she adds
Irani is now planning to move beyond images to video and audio

She wants to be able to reconstruct what people are thinking about or imagining, and the contents of their dreams. “That’s something we don’t have yet,” she says. “But we’re striving to achieve it.” Such a tool might enable people who are “locked in” and completely paralyzed to communicate using their brain activity alone, she says
It could also help scientists unpick some enduring mysteries surrounding the inner workings of our minds, such as what PTSD flashbacks look like

title: How smaller, distributed batteries could help the grid
excerpt: If you want to install a big battery in New York City, you have to cut through a notoriously tough tangle of regulations
body: If you want to install a big battery in New York City, you have to cut through a notoriously tough tangle of regulations
That’s made it difficult to get large energy storage projects on the grid
Faced with those obstacles, some startups are getting creative, finding ways to use relatively small batteries in unexpected places, from induction stovetops to food carts
By deploying these more consumer-focused batteries, the companies are helping people directly, cutting pollution or power bills
And these units, while small on their own, could add up to a lot of capacity
Large, utility-scale battery installations are coming online quickly around the world

But there’s been some pushback from communities—especially population-dense ones like NYC—because of concerns about relatively rare but high-profile battery fires . “The number-one challenge that large-scale centralized energy storage providers have is the fact that their benefits are abstract and their costs are concrete,” said David Hammer, cofounder of PopWheels, at a New York Climate Week event on September 24
PopWheels built a battery-swapping system for delivery drivers who zip around the city on e-bikes
Drivers swap out depleted batteries for fresh ones at a cabinet, avoiding the need to stop and charge
There are about 50 cabinets across New York City, and about 2,500 batteries in circulation, Hammer says
The company recently started providing its batteries to food cart operators, allowing them to replace the gas generators they currently rely on
About four of its batteries can supply five kilowatt-hours of electricity, enough to roughly cover a day’s operation for many carts
Copper, for example, is a company building induction stoves with integrated batteries

The appliances allow residents to cook if the power goes out, and they could also help homeowners avoid expensive electrical upgrades, because the battery provides some of the power when the stove is in use. “We’re not just selling a battery for resilience—we’re selling it for cost savings,” Sam Calisch, cofounder and CEO of Copper, said at the event.   COPPER Other companies, like Every Electric and David Energy are selling plug-in batteries for homes and businesses
Every’s battery is designed to be plugged in to an air-conditioning unit
The company provides the batteries and pays customers to reduce use during high-stress times
David Energy has a similar business model, but focuses on businesses like laundromats, parking garages, and gyms
Because all these companies’ batteries are small or even integrated into another device, they don’t generally require grid upgrades or extensive permitting processes
Just plug them in and enjoy the benefits—similar to the growing model of balcony solar , with small modules that plug in and help offset a home’s or business’s energy demand

The move toward more distributed batteries could be a huge change for the grid. “This is the biggest thing to happen in the power grid sector in the last 20 years,” says James McGinniss, cofounder and CEO of David Energy
If every stove in America were shipped with a battery, it would add up to tens of gigawatts of power, Calisch said
That’s capacity that can be aggregated and tapped when the grid is stressed
As batteries continue to get cheaper, they’ll likely find their way into more corners of our lives, bringing along many benefits
Cleaner air, cheaper power bills—there’s a lot to like

That being said, the need for large-scale energy storage isn’t going to go away—larger installations will do the crucial work of supporting intermittent renewables like wind and solar, so they can help meet more of our quickly growing electricity demand.  But I’m interested to see how far an aggregated horde of stoves, e-bikes, and window AC units could go in helping the grid
The grid is getting more congested, especially in dense cities like New York
Anything that could help avoid summer blackouts is welcome
This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter

title: Christa Pike survived a lethal injection attempt – the latest person to endure a failed execution
url:
<title>Christa Pike survived a lethal injection attempt – the latest person to endure a failed execution</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763438/original/file-20261001-50-w7xxyl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8640%2C5760&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Emergency vehicles arrive at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, Tenn., on Sept. 30, 2026, after Christa Pike&#39;s execution was halted.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/TennesseeExecution/ed9b7642e80e4dae9c585fa5679fdbff/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=Christa%20Pike&amp;currentItemNo=33&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/George Walker IV</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://www.tennessean.com/story/news/crime/2026/09/30/christa-pike-death-penalty-execution-live-updates--live/91994490007/">Christa Pike survived an execution attempt</a> in Tennessee on Sept. 30, 2026, after receiving <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/christa-pike-stay-execution-tennessee.html">two doses of pentobarbital</a>, a lethal drug. Gov. Bill Lee has temporarily suspended executions in the state. </p>

<p>Pike became the first person ever to get <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/us/christa-pike-execution-tennessee">full doses of the drugs intended to kill</a> her and to live nonetheless. But she is not the only person to have survived an execution failure in the Volunteer State.</p>

<p>Tennessee <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/may/26/tony-carruthers-tennessee-execution">set out to execute Tony Carruthers</a> on May 21, 2026, but he lived to tell about it. </p>

<p>Carruthers, who <a href="https://murderpedia.org/male.C/c/carruthers-tony.htm">was sentenced to death for a 1994 triple murder</a>, survived his date with death when the execution team members could find only one suitable vein in which to secure an IV, but not, <a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2026/05/21/tony-carruthers-execution-tennessee-on-hold/90196934007/">as USA Today reports</a>, the “backup line, which is required under the state’s lethal injection protocol.” </p>

<p>After the failed attempt, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee <a href="https://www.tn.gov/governor/news/2026/5/21/gov--lee-grants-temporary-reprieve-for-tony-von-carruthers.html">gave Carruthers a one-year reprieve</a>, a decision the governor did not explain. </p>

<p>What happened to Pike and Carruthers is a reminder that things frequently <a href="https://www.sup.org/books/law/gruesome-spectacles">go wrong in executions</a>, even if in almost all cases the problem is resolved and the execution is completed. </p>

<p>Indeed, in the past 80 years, only eight other people have <a href="https://www.cardozoersj.com/_files/ugd/a6e465_5a9b23ce8ae34dab96415b85942a712f.pdf">had experiences like Carruthers’ and Pike’s</a> and survived execution attempts.</p>

<p>Four of those execution “survivors” <a href="https://www.cardozoersj.com/_files/ugd/a6e465_5a9b23ce8ae34dab96415b85942a712f.pdf">were killed by a second execution</a> attempt, while others escaped that fate. Three others died on death row; one of them after the state agreed not to try to execute him a second time, and one of them is still alive and awaiting his fate. </p>

<p>Having <a href="https://www.amazon.com/When-State-Kills-Punishment-Condition/dp/0691102619">studied capital punishment for decades</a>, I know the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition of “cruel and unusual punishment” has shaped constitutional discussions around failed executions. But so far, courts <a href="https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2009-sep-19-na-execute-redux19-story.html">have not stood in the way</a> when state governments have wanted to try to execute the same man again.</p>

<h2>Not just a lethal injection problem</h2>

<p>Carruthers and Pike survived lethal injection attempts, but execution failures have not been confined to that method. A look at <a href="https://press.umich.edu/Books/F/From-Noose-to-Needle">the history of hanging reveals</a> several instances in which it failed.</p>

<p>In 1833, for example, a hanging in Pennsylvania <a href="https://www.wfmz.com/archive/dni/historys-headlines-ghostly-getters-island/article_c5d18933-d387-50f6-8abd-adaa03e56505.html">failed to kill Charles Getter</a>, who had been sentenced to death for murdering his wife.</p>

<p>“The rope was placed around Getter’s neck. The hangman drew it up fast,” <a href="https://www.amazon.com/Rope-History-Hanged-Amanda-Howard/dp/1742576923">true crime author Amanda Howard notes</a>. “Getter struggled and kicked, choking, before the rope broke, throwing him to the ground.” However, Getter did not die.</p>

<p>The executioner <a href="https://www.amazon.com/Rope-History-Hanged-Amanda-Howard/dp/1742576923">sent someone to look for a stronger rope</a>. This time, <a href="https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-allentown-democrat-some-backstory-on/1441526/">the rope did not break</a> and Getter met “the fate of a murderer.”</p>

<p>In 1894, <a href="https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn86079088/1877-02-17/ed-1/?sp=1">Will Purvis’ hanging also failed</a> when the noose loosened. Instead of dying from a broken neck, Purvis survived, suffering only rope burns on his neck.</p>

<p>Unlike Getter, Purvis <a href="https://carolinafamilyroots.blogspot.com/2012/11/the-hanging-of-innocent-man-will-purvis.html">returned to prison contending that he was innocent</a>. His lawyers unsuccessfully tried to get the courts to prevent a second execution attempt. Purvis remained behind bars until 1898, when Mississippi’s governor pardoned him. Purvis is the only execution survivor ever to receive such grace.</p>

<p>In the late 19th century, <a href="https://www.amazon.com/Executioners-Current-Westinghouse-Invention-Electric/dp/037572446X">the electric chair replaced hanging</a> as the country’s primary execution method, but it did not prevent failed executions. At least once in the 20th century, the electric chair also failed to kill.</p>

<p>In the spring of 1946, the state of Louisiana <a href="https://www.cla.purdue.edu/academic/communication/cspan/ccse/civics-literacy-initiative/4-death-by-installments.html">tried to use it in the execution of Willie Francis</a>, a 16-year-old Black youth who had been convicted of murdering a local sheriff. At the time, the electric chair was said to be <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/116966/executioners-current-by-richard-moran/">the most humane execution method</a>.</p>

<p>But what Francis experienced hardly seemed humane. When <a href="https://www.cla.purdue.edu/academic/communication/cspan/ccse/civics-literacy-initiative/4-death-by-installments.html">the electric current reached</a> him, “He started going into convulsions.” The executioner “flipped the switch again,” but Francis was not killed.</p>

<p>Later, like Purvis, Francis turned to the courts to try to stave off another execution attempt. The decision in his case would set the precedent for how judges would deal with other execution survivors.</p>

<h2>An accident?</h2>

<p>In January 1947, months after Francis survived the electrocution, the U.S. Supreme Court <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/329/459/">gave Louisiana permission to try again</a>. The justices split, with five giving Louisiana the green light and four dissenting.</p>

<p>Justice Stanley Reed’s majority opinion emphasized that what had happened to Francis was accidental and that, without malicious intent, there was no violation of the Eighth Amendment. As he put it, “The fact that an unforeseeable accident prevented the prompt consummation of the sentence cannot, it seems to us, add an element of cruelty to its subsequent execution.”</p>

<p>In his view, “The cruelty against which the constitution protects a convicted man is cruelty ‘inherent’ in the method of punishment, not the ‘necessary suffering’ involved in any method employed to extinguish life humanely.”</p>

<p><a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/329/459/">Justice Harold Burton spoke for the dissenting judges</a>. As he put it: “The intent of the executioner cannot lessen the torture or excuse the result.” A second execution would offend the “fundamental instincts of civilized man.”</p>

<p>Francis was put to death almost a year to the day after his first execution failed.</p>

<p>It would be several decades until <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1984/03/14/us/texas-executes-convicted-killer-who-won-late-reprieve-in-1983.html">another person survived an execution</a>. But the pace of failed executions has only picked up since the start of the 21st century.</p>

<h2>21st century execution survivors</h2>

<p>From 2009 until May 2026, six people <a href="https://www.cardozoersj.com/_files/ugd/a6e465_5a9b23ce8ae34dab96415b85942a712f.pdf">survived failed lethal injection attempts</a>. Romell Broom became the first 21st-century execution survivor when in 2009 the state of Ohio gave up after trying for two hours to find a usable vein in which to secure an IV line.</p>

<p>In his case, <a href="https://www.supremecourt.ohio.gov/rod/docs/pdf/0/2016/2016-ohio-1028.pdf">the Ohio Supreme Court</a>, relying on the Francis precedent, decided that “The insertion of IV lines is merely a preparatory step to the execution.” In its view, Broom’s punishment had not really begun. Therefore, a second execution would not violate the prohibition on double jeopardy or on the imposition of cruel punishment.</p>

<p>But before Ohio could again attempt to execute Broom, <a href="https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/romell-broom-who-survived-botched-execution-dies-of-covid-19-on-ohio-death-row">he died on death row</a> in December 2020 after contracting COVID-19. Another 21st-century execution survivor, Alva Campbell, also <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/alva-campbell-inmate-who-survived-execution-try-dies-ohio-prison-n852961">died on death row</a>.</p>

<p>In 2018, Doyle Hamm <a href="https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/confidential-settlement-leaves-questions-about-alabama-execution-process-unanswered">reached an agreement with the state of Alabama</a> stating that he would not be subject to a second execution after executioners couldn’t access a vein during an attempted lethal injection. Hamm died from cancer in 2021.</p>

<p>However, Alabama succeeded in executing two other execution survivors, <a href="https://eji.org/news/alan-miller-alabama-execution-2024/">Alan Miller</a> and <a href="https://alabamareflector.com/2024/01/25/kenneth-eugene-smith-executed-by-nitrogen-gas-for-1988-murder-for-hire-scheme/">Kenneth Smith</a>, both in 2024. In both cases, they had survived failed lethal injections. </p>

<p>And <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/06/06/us/thomas-creech-idaho-botched-execution.html">Thomas Creech is, like Carruthers and Pike, still alive</a> after lethal injection failure, this time in Idaho. It’s not clear if and when <a href="https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/idaho-federal-judge-grants-stay-of-execution-for-thomas-creech-defense-asks-court-to-bar-death-penalty-for-bryan-kohberger">Idaho will try again to put him to death</a>. If it does, the state will use the firing squad, which <a href="https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/idaho-governor-signs-legislation-authorizing-firing-squad-as-states-primary-execution-method">became its primary execution method</a> on July 1, 2026.</p>

<h2>Carruthers’ fate</h2>

<p>As Carruthers awaits his fate in Tennessee, defense lawyers in the state <a href="https://www.wjhl.com/news/regional/tennessee/days-after-botched-execution-defense-attorneys-call-on-gov-lee-to-halt-all-executions/">have asked Gov. Lee to halt all executions</a> pending a thorough review of its protocol.</p>

            </figcaption>

<p>And as the <a href="https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/tennessees-botched-execution-of-tony-carruthers-raises-questions-about-medical-qualifications-among-concerns-with-innocence-and-due-process">Death Penalty Information Center reports</a>, “attorneys from the Federal Public Defender’s Office filed a new federal lawsuit … to prevent Tennessee from attempting to execute Mr. Carruthers a second time.” </p>

<p>That suit builds on <a href="https://wreg.com/news/tn-lawsuit-claims-lethal-injection-violates-8th-amendment/">litigation filed in March 2025</a> alleging that the administration of lethal injection in Tennessee inflicts cruel and unusual punishment.</p>

<p>Only time will tell if the judges who hear those cases will be persuaded by what Justice Burton <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/329/459/">wrote in the Francis case</a>: “Although the failure of the first attempt, in the present case was unintended, the reapplication of the electric current will be intentional … The present case demonstrates that, today, two separate applications are sufficiently ‘cruel and unusual’ to be prohibited.”</p>

<p>When the state, Burton <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/329/459/">explained</a>, seeks to execute someone, it has a duty “to make sure that there (is) no failure.”</p>

<title>Dozens of men failed to stop an alleged gang rape at Cornell – here’s the misperception that keeps bystanders from intervening and how to short-circuit it</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763467/original/file-20261001-50-xw7r40.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=897%2C865%2C7431%2C4954&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People may quash their own beliefs to fit in with what they think the group believes.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/yorkcollege-fraternity-students-in-a-morning-party-of-binge-news-photo/1192105065">Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis News via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As an undergrad student decades ago, I attended a dorm presentation describing the importance of giving and receiving sexual consent. The workshop leaders explained that if your partner said “no” or “stop” but you proceeded to have sex anyway, it was considered rape.</p>

<p>A high-profile athlete on campus raised his hand and said, in utter disbelief, “That can’t be right. By that definition, everyone I’ve ever had sex with I’ve raped.”</p>

<p>I was horrified by his comment, but most students laughed. He clearly saw nothing wrong with the view he’d expressed, presumably believing it was widely shared.</p>

<p>I immediately thought of this experience when I heard about the alleged sexual assault committed by <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/nyregion/cornell-university-rape-investigation-chi-phi-fraternity.html">seven fraternity members at Cornell University</a>. <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=-dCo5lYAAAAJ">As a social psychologist</a>, and the author of a book examining <a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674271111">why so-called good people stay silent</a> in the face of problematic behavior, what I find most tragic about the events at Cornell is that <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/video/woman-cornell-told-police-raped-3-weeks-after-alleged-incident/">reportedly over 50 men on a group chat</a> <a href="https://www.cornellsun.com/article/2026/09/tccsuykuvb4z">learned about the assault as it was happening</a>. Yet there’s been no public report that any of them tried to stop the assault, help the victim or contact campus or local police departments. </p>

<p>This type of inaction is very common. In about <a href="https://apnews.com/article/21fe7b026c0b4e779a6cd67f9e592d02">one-third of sexual assaults</a>, at least one other person is present who potentially could intervene but in most instances chooses not to. Why?</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763469/original/file-20261001-50-p6u9b8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Blurry image of a crowded dancefloor of young adults" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763469/original/file-20261001-50-p6u9b8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763469/original/file-20261001-50-p6u9b8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=401&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763469/original/file-20261001-50-p6u9b8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=401&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763469/original/file-20261001-50-p6u9b8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=401&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763469/original/file-20261001-50-p6u9b8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763469/original/file-20261001-50-p6u9b8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763469/original/file-20261001-50-p6u9b8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A group’s norms can be driven by a minority who are actually out of step with what most think is right.</span>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Misperceiving that you’re the only one</h2>

<p>Data suggests a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1891/vivi.17.1.73.33638">minority of men actually commit sexual assault</a>. Researchers estimate about <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1524838019860619">6.5% of male college students</a> in the United States and Canada have committed rape. Yet many men who find sexual violence offensive mistakenly believe that other men do not. </p>

<p>Undergraduate men in one study reported their <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/a0039443">beliefs about common rape myths</a>, such as “If a girl doesn’t physically fight back, you can’t really say it was rape,” and “If a girl goes to a room alone with a guy at a party, it is her own fault if she is raped.” Researchers then asked participants how they thought both their close friends and average male college students would answer these same questions.</p>

<p>The results provided clear evidence that college men have skewed views of what those around them are thinking. Most students saw their classmates and friends as more supportive of rape myths than they themselves were. </p>

<p>Unfortunately, believing that other men generally accept sexual violence – even when this belief is wrong – <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0886260509334400">inhibits their willingness to intervene</a> to stop such behavior when they encounter it. In fact, men’s beliefs about their peers’ attitudes are a stronger predictor of their willingness to intervene than their own stated attitudes about sexual aggression. </p>

<h2>What’s behind these mistaken beliefs</h2>

<p>Men who underestimate their peers’ discomfort with sexually aggressive behavior often fear the consequences of calling out problematic views or intervening in the face of inappropriate behavior. The most common reason male college students give for failing to intervene in situations involving sexual violence is a fear of being laughed at or ridiculed – in particular, <a href="https://doi.org/10.3149/jms.1601.3">a desire not to appear weak to other men</a>. </p>

<p>Men who actually commit assault also tend to overestimate support for such behavior. Not surprisingly, men who report having committed sexual assault <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/a0039443">believe that other men are more accepting</a> of such behavior and have engaged in such behavior themselves. </p>

<p>This <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60238-5">assumed support leads them to feel comfortable</a> describing problematic behavior, which leads other men to believe that sexual violence is more common, and more accepted, than it actually is.</p>

<h2>Resetting a social norm</h2>

<p>Given the consistent evidence that men wrongly believe that most men are more comfortable with sexual violence than they themselves are, the challenge is not to change the social norm. It’s <a href="https://archive.nytimes.com/opinionator.blogs.nytimes.com/2013/03/27/the-destructive-influence-of-imaginary-peers/">getting people to see what it actually already is</a>.</p>

<p>Correcting such misperceptions can go a long way toward reducing sexual violence. First-year male college students who participate in a 90-minute sexual assault prevention program – focused on refuting rape myths, increasing awareness of the importance of consent, and correcting misperceptions about other men’s attitudes and behaviors – report <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1077801211409727">reduced levels of sexual aggression</a> themselves four months later. </p>

<p>These programs work in two ways. First, men who receive accurate information about what other men actually believe are less inhibited about speaking out and intervening. Second, men who are at risk of engaging in sexual aggression may change their intentions after learning that their peers do not support such behavior. </p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Loyal support can be recast as helping a friend do the right thing and stay safe.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/diverse-group-of-friends-hug-one-another-royalty-free-image/1411288800">SDI Productions/E+ via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>At the same time, men in tight-knit groups feel considerable pressure to show loyalty to other group members, which may lead to ignoring bad behavior committed by their peers.</p>

<p>But the underlying dynamics of peer influence can help shift group norms from protecting group members by staying silent to stepping in to prevent bad behavior. One college football player described looking out for his teammates, even if that meant interrupting a potential sexual encounter: “Maybe you don’t get the girl, but <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2014/02/09/education/edlife/stepping-up-to-stop-sexual-assault.html">you’ll keep your scholarship and still be on the team</a>.” </p>

<h2>Learn strategies for intervening</h2>

<p>Another approach for preventing sexual assault is to learn strategies for intervening. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/jcop.10078">Bystander intervention programs</a> emphasize the importance of stopping bad behavior before it escalates, teach specific skills for intervening, and remind people that everyone has a responsibility to prevent sexual violence. </p>

<p>Students who participate in such programs are more confident in their ability to intervene and more willing to do so. Most importantly, rates of sexual violence are markedly lower on campuses that have implemented these programs. For example, one study found that experiences of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1077801214545284">sexual harassment and stalking were 11% lower</a> and that instances of unwanted sexual activity with women who were too drunk or high to stop them were as much as 17% lower.</p>

<p>It’s tempting to read about the Cornell case and assume the apparent inaction in the face of problematic behavior is uniquely a problem at one college, or only with members of fraternities, or only college students. But the reality is that pretty much everyone has been in situations where they’ve seen potentially problematic behavior and failed to speak up. </p>

<p>Understanding the very normal psychological factors that lead people to misperceive what others are actually thinking and feeling – and learning specific strategies for intervening – can make a real difference.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293321/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
