<title>Dan Rather has followed the news wherever he goes, in a career that highlights 75 years of evolving journalism</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/700907/original/file-20251106-64-brl4fu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=40%2C0%2C1911%2C1274&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">CBS News anchor Dan Rather rehearses for election night coverage on Nov. 3, 2000, in New York.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/MediaCBSDanRather/26c7534b4e7541fe86189bcbe335eb59/photo">AP Photo/Mark Lennihan</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In television news, there are two roles in front of the camera: reporter and anchor. </p>

<p>During four decades at CBS, Dan Rather played both roles. On March 9, 1981, he <a href="https://danratherjournalist.org/anchorman/cbs-anchor-desk.html">took over the position</a> of nightly news anchor from Walter Cronkite, one of the most influential faces in network television. Although Rather held that job for 24 years, first and foremost he embraced being a reporter. </p>

<p>Today, as his 95th birthday birthday approaches on Oct. 31, Rather remains engaged with news as a <a href="https://substack.com/@steady">social media commentator</a>, with plenty to say about the Trump administration and the state of journalism.</p>

<p>Rather began as a regional reporter in Texas and became chief of the network’s Southern bureau in 1963. In the first of many high-profile career moments, he <a href="https://gwtoday.gwu.edu/dan-rather-and-marvin-kalb-reflect-jfk-assassination">organized the network’s local coverage</a> of President John F. Kennedy’s Nov. 22, 1963, visit to Dallas, where Kennedy was assassinated.</p>

<p>After covering the Nixon White House, the Vietnam War and other domestic and international stories, Rather became one of television’s “Big Three” nightly news anchors in 1981. For the next two decades, Rather on CBS, Peter Jennings on ABC and Tom Brokaw on NBC, were prominent faces of the last era in which legacy media companies truly set the news agenda.</p>

<p>In his reporting tenure, Dan Rather repeatedly tangled with U.S. presidents. He brought that reporter’s attitude to the anchor role. Rather didn’t just preside over news stories – he was immersed in their preparation and aware of their potential impact. </p>

<p>I <a href="https://uicollaboratory.uic.edu/2322-walter-podrazik">teach communication</a> and have written about <a href="https://press.syr.edu/supressbooks/6663/watching-tv-3/">the history of television and the intersection of media and politics</a>. In my view, the most-cited moments in Rather’s long career reflect the on-edge, on-the-scene, news-gathering spirit of <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/pictures/edward-r-murrow/2/">legendary CBS newsman Edward R. Murrow</a>, rather than the avuncular style of a corporate American media host. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/31ERhYvDDw0?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Dan Rather reports from Dealey Plaza in Dallas, the site of President John F. Kennedy’s assassination, on Nov. 23, 1963, the day after the shooting.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Confronting the powerful</h2>

<p>Murrow first became known for reporting directly from the London Blitz bombings via radio in 1940 and 1941. At home through the 1950s and 1960s, Murrow delivered unflinching TV documentary reports on subjects that included <a href="https://www.billdownscbs.com/2015/11/edward-r-murrow-vs-senator-joseph.html">Sen. Joseph McCarthy’s pursuit of alleged communists</a> in the federal government and <a href="https://www.npr.org/2014/05/31/317364146/in-confronting-poverty-harvest-of-shame-reaped-praise-and-criticism">harsh working conditions faced by migrant farmworkers</a>.</p>

<p>As a reporter, Rather also covered stories with major national impact. Following the Kennedy assassination, he solidified his credentials as CBS’s White House correspondent during the Johnson and Nixon administrations and, in 1966, he was sent at his request to report from Vietnam. </p>

<p>Back stateside, Rather covered the divisive and bitter 1968 presidential campaign. As a determined floor correspondent at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, he was knocked down on camera by security guards while trying to interview a Georgia delegate whom the guards were removing from the convention floor. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/3ByoTxuikls?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">In the first two minutes of this video, Dan Rather is knocked down by security guards while reporting at the 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Rather found his strongest reporting voice during the Nixon administration, pressing for details about the Watergate break-in and subsequent White House efforts to cover up the episode. His questions began to venture into the sensitive topics of potential resignation or even impeachment.</p>

<p>Over time, Rather was cast as Nixon’s most prominent onscreen adversary. When Nixon resigned in August 1974, Rather acquired a lasting reputation for helping to hold a U.S. president accountable. </p>

<h2>Finding stories everywhere</h2>

<p>After Nixon’s resignation, Rather’s presence at CBS News grew. He served as weekend news anchor and chief correspondent for the documentary series “<a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/cbs-reports/">CBS Reports</a>,” and he joined the weekly news magazine “<a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/60-minutes/">60 Minutes</a>” in 1975.</p>

<p>One of his most-discussed reports was a 1980 story on the Russian occupation of Afghanistan. To cover the war firsthand, Rather and his team dressed in local garb and crossed the border from Pakistan into Afghanistan, where they interviewed resistance fighters and visited battle sites.</p>

<p>Critics praised the segment for showing U.S. audiences the stakes in a faraway conflict; they also rebuked Rather and “60 Minutes” for showboating. Washington Post media critic <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1980/04/07/gunga-dan/88e47b5f-49cd-4934-ae0d-aedda4a9d282/">Tom Shales wrote</a>, “It’s hard to decide whether Murrow is smiling down approvingly or spinning in his grave.”</p>

<p>In 1981, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2004/11/24/business/a-reporteranchor-who-blazed-a-trail-of-his-own.html">Rather won the competition to succeed Walter Cronkite</a> as “CBS Evening News” anchor, a position he would hold for 24 years. </p>

<p>Rather’s style and demeanor were noticeably different from Cronkite’s reassuring cadence. Even behind the anchor desk, Rather’s inquisitive manner and reporter’s instincts for confrontation were well known. Those traits could be seen as either powerful assets or indicators of biased coverage.</p>

<p>Rather also continued to report, through CBS vehicles such as “<a href="https://www.cbs.com/shows/48_hours/">48 Hours</a>,” a show that investigated crime and justice stories, and the spinoff show “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0182552/">60 Minutes II</a>.” His pursuit of international and domestic stories earned <a href="https://danratherjournalist.org/about-dan/awards.html">numerous Emmy and Peabody awards</a> – more than a dozen in the 1980s alone – and he also received special honors, including his 2004 induction into the Television Academy Hall of Fame.</p>

The interview was one of the first Mandela gave upon his release on Feb. 11, 1990, after serving 27 years in prison.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/NelsonMandelaInterview/dbdd53ae87654a7da41314db1e1cc688/photo?vs=false">AP Photo/John Parkin</a></span>

<h2>Exit from CBS</h2>

<p>Rather’s trajectory changed abruptly after he reported a 2004 “60 Minutes II” segment about then-President George W. Bush’s service in the Texas Air National Guard in 1968-1974. The segment raised questions about whether Bush – whose father was former president George H.W. Bush – had received preferential treatment that kept him from being sent to fight in the Vietnam War.</p>

<p>Critics challenged the authenticity of some documents that CBS cited in the report, and an external review panel concluded that the network <a href="https://blog.smu.edu/2004-election/killian-documents/">had failed to authenticate them properly</a>. The network apologized; Rather defended the report initially but <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/dan-rather-statement-on-memos/TH">conceded after several weeks</a> that the materials should not have been used. The debacle became known as “Rathergate.”</p>

<p>Rather’s CBS contract <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2006/06/21/business/media/21rather.html">was not renewed</a>. He left the anchor chair in 2005 and the network in 2006, asserting in his departing press statement, “I will do the work I love elsewhere.” </p>

<p>Before leaving CBS, Rather urged citizens and journalists alike to <a href="https://www.seattlepi.com/seattlenews/article/demand-solid-news-rather-urges-1193799.php">take on the tough battles</a>. “Whether it’s City Hall, the Statehouse or the White House, part of our job is to speak truth to power,” Rather said in a 2006 speech in Seattle. </p>

<h2>New platforms</h2>

<p>Cable news offered Rather an alternative. Over the next 15 years he hosted several <a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0837293/">in-depth reporting</a> and <a href="https://axs.tv/show/the-big-interview-with-dan-rather/">interview programs</a> on cable channels. There, he embraced being a news reporter who could call his own shots and criticize people in positions of power in politics and business.</p>

<p>In his 80s, Rather took to social media, attracting hundreds of thousands of followers via <a href="https://www.facebook.com/theDanRather/">Facebook</a>, <a href="https://x.com/DanRather">the social platform X, formerly Twitter</a>, and <a href="https://steady.substack.com/">Steady</a>, a newsletter distributed via the Substack platform. He quickly adopted the language of short-burst online communication, using snark and style in the service of delivering solid journalism.</p>



<h2>Speaking truth to the press</h2>

<p>Today, the Trump administration is widely viewed as <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-moves-against-media-outlets-mirror-authoritarian-approaches-to-silencing-dissent">waging war on the mainstream media</a>. President Donald Trump regularly <a href="https://www.vanityfair.com/news/story/trump-rally-man-attacks-journalists">calls journalists the “enemy of the people</a>,” has tightly limited reporters’ access at the White House and the Pentagon, and has <a href="https://www.axios.com/2025/07/22/trump-lawsuits-wsj-npr-pbs">sued numerous media outlets</a> for what he calls unfair or defamatory coverage. </p>

<p>In response, many large media companies are taking steps that critics see as <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2025/06/05/marty-baron-jeff-bezos-trump-00389931">pulling punches or currying favor</a> with the Trump White House. For example, in the fall of 2025 CBS News <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/05/business/cbs-face-the-nation-editing-rules.html">adopted new rules</a> that bar editing recorded interviews before they air. </p>

<p>This step came after the network’s parent company <a href="https://www.ap.org/news-highlights/spotlights/2025/paramount-will-pay-16-million-in-settlement-with-trump-over-60-minutes-interview/">paid Trump US$16 million</a> to settle a lawsuit over its editing of a 2024 interview with Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris. CBS also hired Kenneth Weinstein, a prominent conservative and former think tank executive, for <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/08/business/media/cbs-news-ombudsman-kenneth-weinstein.html">a new ombudsman position</a>.</p>

<p>In <a href="https://steady.substack.com/p/maga-tested-trump-approved-news">a Substack post</a>, Rather called the changes evidence that CBS “has tipped over the precipice: that corporate overlords in concert with an autocratic president are demolishing support for independent journalism in favor of financial gain, and in so doing undermining a key foundation of our democracy.” His warning echoed Murrow’s famous 1958 speech urging broadcast leaders to use the power of the medium to teach, illuminate and inspire, rather than letting it become “nothing but <a href="https://www.rtdna.org/murrows-famous-wires-and-lights-in-a-box">wires and lights in a box</a>.”</p>

<p>Dan Rather has pursued that mission throughout his career, even as the players and technologies have changed. He has consistently embraced the challenges, and satisfaction, of being a journalist intent on holding powerful people accountable – including the heads of news organizations.</p>

<p><em>Harry Castleman, co-author with Walter Podrazik of “<a href="https://press.syr.edu/supressbooks/6663/watching-tv-3/">Watching TV: American Television, Season by Season</a>,” contributed to this article.</em></p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/265967/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Walter Podrazik is a board member at the Library of American Broadcasting Foundation. He is Television Curator at the Museum of Broadcast Communications in Chicago, and serves on the development for its current Johnny Carson Centennial and Evolution of Late Night exhibits. He is president of the Society of Midland Authors. </span></em></p></content>
    <summary>Dan Rather anchored the ‘CBS Evening News’ for over 20 years, starting on March 9, 1981. But he always seemed more in his element as a reporter, and now as a news analyst on social media.</summary>

body: CBS News anchor Dan Rather rehearses for election night coverage on Nov. 3, 2000, in New York
AP Photo/Mark Lennihan In television news, there are two roles in front of the camera: reporter and anchor
During four decades at CBS, Dan Rather played both roles
On March 9, 1981, he took over the position of nightly news anchor from Walter Cronkite, one of the most influential faces in network television
Although Rather held that job for 24 years, first and foremost he embraced being a reporter

Today, as his 95th birthday birthday approaches on Oct. 31, Rather remains engaged with news as a social media commentator , with plenty to say about the Trump administration and the state of journalism
Rather began as a regional reporter in Texas and became chief of the network’s Southern bureau in 1963
In the first of many high-profile career moments, he organized the network’s local coverage of President John F
Kennedy’s Nov. 22, 1963, visit to Dallas, where Kennedy was assassinated
After covering the Nixon White House, the Vietnam War and other domestic and international stories, Rather became one of television’s “Big Three” nightly news anchors in 1981
For the next two decades, Rather on CBS, Peter Jennings on ABC and Tom Brokaw on NBC, were prominent faces of the last era in which legacy media companies truly set the news agenda
In his reporting tenure, Dan Rather repeatedly tangled with U.S. presidents
He brought that reporter’s attitude to the anchor role
Rather didn’t just preside over news stories – he was immersed in their preparation and aware of their potential impact
I teach communication and have written about the history of television and the intersection of media and politics
In my view, the most-cited moments in Rather’s long career reflect the on-edge, on-the-scene, news-gathering spirit of legendary CBS newsman Edward R
Murrow , rather than the avuncular style of a corporate American media host
Dan Rather reports from Dealey Plaza in Dallas, the site of President John F
Kennedy’s assassination, on Nov. 23, 1963, the day after the shooting
Confronting the powerful Murrow first became known for reporting directly from the London Blitz bombings via radio in 1940 and 1941
At home through the 1950s and 1960s, Murrow delivered unflinching TV documentary reports on subjects that included Sen
Joseph McCarthy’s pursuit of alleged communists in the federal government and harsh working conditions faced by migrant farmworkers
As a reporter, Rather also covered stories with major national impact

Following the Kennedy assassination, he solidified his credentials as CBS’s White House correspondent during the Johnson and Nixon administrations and, in 1966, he was sent at his request to report from Vietnam
Back stateside, Rather covered the divisive and bitter 1968 presidential campaign

As a determined floor correspondent at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, he was knocked down on camera by security guards while trying to interview a Georgia delegate whom the guards were removing from the convention floor
In the first two minutes of this video, Dan Rather is knocked down by security guards while reporting at the 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago
Rather found his strongest reporting voice during the Nixon administration, pressing for details about the Watergate break-in and subsequent White House efforts to cover up the episode
His questions began to venture into the sensitive topics of potential resignation or even impeachment
Over time, Rather was cast as Nixon’s most prominent onscreen adversary
When Nixon resigned in August 1974, Rather acquired a lasting reputation for helping to hold a U.S. president accountable
Finding stories everywhere After Nixon’s resignation, Rather’s presence at CBS News grew
He served as weekend news anchor and chief correspondent for the documentary series “ CBS Reports ,” and he joined the weekly news magazine “ 60 Minutes ” in 1975
One of his most-discussed reports was a 1980 story on the Russian occupation of Afghanistan
To cover the war firsthand, Rather and his team dressed in local garb and crossed the border from Pakistan into Afghanistan, where they interviewed resistance fighters and visited battle sites
Critics praised the segment for showing U.S. audiences the stakes in a faraway conflict; they also rebuked Rather and “60 Minutes” for showboating

Washington Post media critic Tom Shales wrote , “It’s hard to decide whether Murrow is smiling down approvingly or spinning in his grave.” In 1981, Rather won the competition to succeed Walter Cronkite as “CBS Evening News” anchor, a position he would hold for 24 years
Rather’s style and demeanor were noticeably different from Cronkite’s reassuring cadence
Even behind the anchor desk, Rather’s inquisitive manner and reporter’s instincts for confrontation were well known
Those traits could be seen as either powerful assets or indicators of biased coverage

<title>From suicide bombers to positions of authority – the changing role of women in jihadi groups</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763176/original/file-20260930-82-bwt636.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=139%2C0%2C2416%2C1611&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Women are taking a more active role in jihadi organizations.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://deeply.thenewhumanitarian.org/syria/articles/2014/07/15/in-raqqa-an-all-female-isis-brigade-cracks-down-on-local-women">Syria Deeply/https://deeply.thenewhumanitarian.org/syria</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Khadra Essa, a Somali-born Dutch citizen operating in Syria under the name Umm Qaqa al-Somali, is a wanted woman. </p>

<p>On Sept. 14, 2026, the U.S. State Department <a href="https://x.com/RFJ_USA/status/2099528840544440737">again publicized</a> its offer of up to US$5 million <a href="https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/khadra-essa/">for information about her whereabouts</a>, having first offered a reward  in April 2025.</p>

<p>The notice <a href="https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/khadra-essa/">describes Essa</a> as the chief sharia instructor of Khatiba Nusaybah, or ISIS-NK, an all-female Islamic State combat battalion formed in Raqqa, Syria, in 2016 to recruit, organize and train female fighters.</p>

<p>The United States <a href="https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/khadra-essa/">alleges she received</a> formal training in weapons, explosives and suicide operations. The State Department notice claims Essa “taught ISIS extremist ideology that justified suicide operations and killing of civilians,” recruited members, made orders that resulted in assaults and murder, and “led a group that violently enforced sharia law against women.” There is a <a href="https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/kidnapping-of-yusuf-and-zahra-shikder/">separate State Department notice</a> for information leading to the location and return of two American children allegedly taken by Essa after the death of their mother – an Islamic State group recruit – in 2019.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A poster shows a women face and details of a financial reward." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762578/original/file-20260928-60-dyhiz1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762578/original/file-20260928-60-dyhiz1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=352&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762578/original/file-20260928-60-dyhiz1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=352&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762578/original/file-20260928-60-dyhiz1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=352&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762578/original/file-20260928-60-dyhiz1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=442&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762578/original/file-20260928-60-dyhiz1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=442&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762578/original/file-20260928-60-dyhiz1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=442&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The U.S. Department of State has offered a $5 million reward for Khadra Essa.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/khadra-essa/">U.S. Department of State</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As a <a href="https://extremism.gwu.edu/sara-harmouch">terrorism researcher</a> who studies how militant groups organize and adapt, I’ve examined U.S. and European court records, sanctions and reward notices, as well as jihadi groups’ own Arabic-language publications, to trace how women’s roles inside armed movements have evolved. </p>

<p>For <a href="https://www.ipcs.org/comm_select.php?articleNo=1118">as long as</a> modern terrorism has existed, women <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/paris-attacks-hasna-aitboulahcen-not-the-first-female-suicide-bomber/">have been known to fight</a> and <a href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/commentary/2005/12/the-bomber-behind-the-veil.html">carry</a> <a href="https://www.americanprogress.org/article/the-unaddressed-threat-of-female-suicide-bombers/">out attacks</a>. But I’ve observed a newer development whereby women’s organizational authority in jihadi groups has been increasingly formalized. Indeed, women are occupying defined roles in which they train, recruit, discipline or direct other members, or manage functions on which the organization depends.</p>

<h2>Learning from secular groups</h2>

<p>Two decades ago, the political scientist Brigitte Nacos <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10576100500180352#d1e797">surveyed how women</a> in armed groups were understood. Women had long been leaders and chief ideologues in secular movements – such as in <a href="https://www.fbi.gov/history/cases-and-criminals/weather-underground-bombings">the Weather Underground</a> in the United States, <a href="https://digitalcommons.usf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1005&amp;context=jss">Italy’s Red Brigades</a>, <a href="https://www.dw.com/en/red-army-faction-raf/t-72019175/page-1">Germany’s Red Army Faction</a> and the <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/ethnic-and-cultural-studies/eta-terrorist-group/">Basque separatist group ETA</a>. </p>

<p>In jihadi movements, by contrast, women were rarely presented as people with formal authority over other members or organizational functions. Rather, such groups, exploiting the perception of women as <a href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/commentary/2005/12/the-bomber-behind-the-veil.html">less of a security threat</a>, primarily saw women’s active role in offensive operations as that of a conveyor of bombs.</p>

<p>It was a tactic that had already taken hold in secular militant movements. The Syrian Social Nationalist Party used <a href="https://www.arabnews.com/opinion/how-terrorist-groups-use-women-as-suicide-bombers-1025401">Sana'a Mehaidli</a> in a <a href="https://www.reuters.com/article/world/timeline-female-suicide-bombers-idUSTRE62T3WX/">suicide attack</a> in Lebanon in 1985; in 1991, a female <a href="https://mappingmilitants.org/profiles/liberation-tigers-of-tamil-elam">Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam</a> <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/19472490903387191">operative</a> known as Dhanu <a href="https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/rajiv-gandhi-assassination-case-explained-supreme-court-releases-convicts-8262742/">assassinated</a> Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi; and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party <a href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/1996/07/01/suicide-bomber-kills-9-soldiers-in-turkey/">began</a> deploying <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1996/07/03/world/kurdish-suicide-bomber-kills-9-turkish-soldiers.html?pagewanted=1">female bombers</a> in the 1990s.</p>

<p>By the early 2000s, Palestinian militant groups, including jihadists, were also using female suicide bombers. In January 2002, Wafa Idris <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/512624">died in Jerusalem</a> while killing one man and wounding about 50 people. She is <a href="https://www.inss.org.il/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Female-Suicide-Bombers-25-41.pdf">widely remembered</a> as the first Palestinian woman to carry out a suicide bombing, although <a href="https://www.inss.org.il/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Female-Suicide-Bombers-25-41.pdf">accounts indicate</a> that the device <a href="https://www.inss.org.il/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Female-Suicide-Bombers-25-41.pdf">may have detonated unexpectedly</a>. Four more female suicide bombings <a href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/commentary/2005/12/the-bomber-behind-the-veil.html">followed within months</a> of that attack.</p>

<p>The Palestinian militant group Hamas <a href="https://www.files.ethz.ch/isn/91112/2006-08_Female%20Suicide%20Bombers_complete%20document.pdf">initially</a> <a href="https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/middle-east/woman-suicide-bomber-rejected-by-hamas-9196125.html">resisted</a> using women in suicide attacks but <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10576100500180352#d1e797">relented</a> in 2004.</p>

<p>Its spiritual leader, Ahmed Yassin, explained the change in <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10576100500180352#d1e797">tactical terms</a>: “It could be that a man would not be able to reach the target, and that’s why they had to use a woman.”</p>

<h2>Beyond the bomber</h2>

<p>Within a few years, <a href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/commentary/2005/12/the-bomber-behind-the-veil.html">jihadi groups in Iraq</a>, <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/paris-attacks-hasna-aitboulahcen-not-the-first-female-suicide-bomber/">Jordan</a> and <a href="https://www.france24.com/en/20101226-obama-condemns-pakistan-suicide-attack-female-bomber-burqa">Pakistan</a> were also using female suicide bombers.</p>

<p>But it was the Nigerian-based Boko Haram <a href="https://adf-magazine.com/2018/05/boko-haram-turns-to-women-children-as-suicide-bombers/">that has</a> <a href="https://ctc.westpoint.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Exploding-Stereotypes-1.pdf">scaled the practice</a> beyond any precedent. Research by the <a href="https://ctc.westpoint.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Exploding-Stereotypes.pdf">Combating Terrorism Center</a> identified 434 bombers across 238 suicide attacks between April 2011 and June 2017 – at least 56% of them women.</p>

<p>These cases largely placed women at the operational end of the process. Women carried the bomb or reached the target, but they were far less visible in positions that selected personnel, supplied doctrine, trained operatives or managed the organization itself.</p>

<p>That conservative position initially guided groups such as al-Qaida.</p>

<p>In December 2009, Umayma al-Zawahiri, wife of al-Qaida’s then deputy leader, <a href="https://www.academia.edu/10589334/The_Mujahidaat_Tracing_the_Early_Female_Warriors_of_Islam">published</a> a “Letter to My Muslim Sisters.” It <a href="https://www.academia.edu/10589334/The_Mujahidaat_Tracing_the_Early_Female_Warriors_of_Islam">allowed women</a> to fund operations, gather information and, in principle, carry out a suicide operation, while insisting their principal role was to raise fighters’ children, manage their homes and keep their secrets.</p>

<p>But jihadi propaganda began to stretch the language used for women. </p>

<p>In 2014, the Swahili-language magazine Al-Ghurabaa – aligned with al-Shabaab in Somalia – <a href="https://calebweiss7.substack.com/p/jihadi-archives-al-shabaabs-glorification">published an article</a> titled “Mujahidah Leaders.” Translated and analyzed by <a href="https://x.com/caleb_weiss7">Caleb Weiss</a>, a researcher focused on jihadism in Africa, the magazine declared that “we sisters too have our own leaders.” It presented Aafia Siddiqui – a Pakistani neuroscientist <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/topic/person/aafia-siddiqui">convicted in 2010</a> of attempting to <a href="https://www.justice.gov/archive/opa/pr/2008/August/siddiqui-aafia-complaint.pdf">kill</a> U.S. military and law enforcement personnel – and suspected mass murderer <a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b03bfszq">Samantha Lewthwaite</a> as women to emulate.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A laptop shows a page with a woman's face on it." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762580/original/file-20260928-60-foa65l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762580/original/file-20260928-60-foa65l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762580/original/file-20260928-60-foa65l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762580/original/file-20260928-60-foa65l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762580/original/file-20260928-60-foa65l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762580/original/file-20260928-60-foa65l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762580/original/file-20260928-60-foa65l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">An Interpol ‘Red Notice’ for the arrest of terrorism suspect Samantha Lewthwaite on Sept. 26, 2013.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/view-of-a-laptop-computer-screen-showing-the-interpol-news-photo/181924099?adppopup=true">Oli Scarff/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The rhetoric reflected a broader reality: Women in al-Shabaab <a href="https://jamestown.org/asset-or-victims-a-portrait-of-women-within-al-shabaab/">had already served</a> as recruiters, financiers, couriers and intelligence collectors, even if the movement rarely placed them in formal command positions.</p>

<h2>Expanding women’s roles</h2>

<p>The Islamic State group, meanwhile, was beginning to give some women a more concrete form of authority. </p>

<p>In February 2014 it <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/26473339.pdf?refreqid=fastly-default%3A41ad11c12efd04bc9bc64298b9d75000&amp;ab_segments=&amp;initiator=&amp;acceptTC=1">announced the formation</a> of the <a href="https://georgetownsecuritystudiesreview.org/2021/05/13/isiss-female-morality-police/">all-female al-Khansaa Brigade</a> in Syria. The <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/26473339.pdf">unit emerged</a> partly from a practical security problem: Men disguised in women’s clothing had carried out attacks against Islamic State group commanders, creating a need for women who could search women at checkpoints. Its <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/26473339.pdf?">responsibilities expanded</a> into intelligence gathering, law enforcement, recruitment and policing other women. </p>

<p>They could detain and punish other women, but their authority stopped there. </p>

<p>The brigade occupied an “authoritative position” while <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/26473339.pdf?refreqid=fastly-default%3A41ad11c12efd04bc9bc64298b9d75000&amp;ab_segments=&amp;initiator=&amp;acceptTC=1">remaining unable</a> to challenge Islamic State group policy. </p>

<p>That authority coexisted with a doctrine that still <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2015/feb/05/jihadist-girl-marry-liberation-failed-islamic-state">placed women primarily in the home</a>. A 2015 ISIS <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/26473339.pdf">manifesto permitted</a> women to fight only in <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/26473339.pdf?refreqid=fastly-default%3A41ad11c12efd04bc9bc64298b9d75000&amp;ab_segments=&amp;initiator=&amp;acceptTC=1">exceptional circumstances</a>, principally when Muslim territory was under attack and there were not enough men to defend it.</p>

<p>As Islamic State group territory came under growing pressure, that justification widened. In December 2016 the group’s Arabic newsletter al-Naba <a href="https://ctc.westpoint.edu/the-mujahidat-dilemma-female-combatants-and-the-islamic-state/">published</a> an article titled “I Will Die While Islam Is Glorious,” arguing that jihad was as necessary for a woman as for a man.</p>

<p>By July 2017 the <a href="https://ctc.westpoint.edu/the-mujahidat-dilemma-female-combatants-and-the-islamic-state/">group’s magazine</a> <a href="https://jihadology.net/2017/07/13/new-release-of-the-islamic-states-magazine-rome-11/">Rumiyah</a> was calling on women to rise “with courage and sacrifice in this war.” </p>

<p>The <a href="https://ctc.westpoint.edu/the-mujahidat-dilemma-female-combatants-and-the-islamic-state/">article turned to</a> the 14th-century figure of Nusaybah bint Ka'ab for justification. Also known as Umm Umara, the companion of prophet Muhammad <a href="https://ctc.westpoint.edu/the-mujahidat-dilemma-female-combatants-and-the-islamic-state/">took up arms</a> at the Battle of Uhud. Uhud was a defensive battle, making Nusayba a useful precedent for movements that otherwise restricted women’s participation in combat.</p>

<h2>Becoming named authorities</h2>

<p>The next development came with a different all-female unit. In late 2016 the Islamic State group <a href="https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/american-woman-who-led-isis-battalion-sentenced-20-years">approved the formation of</a> Khatiba Nusaybah, a military battalion composed of female members.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/american-woman-who-led-isis-battalion-sentenced-20-years">Allison Fluke-Ekren</a>, a former Kansas resident who had already organized an Islamic State group women’s center in Raqqa, became the battalion’s leader and organizer. She <a href="https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/american-woman-who-led-isis-battalion-sentenced-20-years">trained more than 100 women and girls</a> in the use of automatic rifles, grenades and suicide belts, according to the U.S. Justice Department. After being <a href="https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/american-woman-who-led-isis-battalion-charged-providing-material-support-terrorist">apprehended</a> in Syria, she was <a href="https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/american-woman-who-led-isis-battalion-charged-providing-material-support-terrorist">transferred</a> to FBI custody in January 2022. She pleaded guilty that June and was <a href="https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/american-woman-who-led-isis-battalion-sentenced-20-years">sentenced in federal court</a> in Virginia to 20 years in prison.</p>

<p>Whereas al-Khansaa had exercised coercive authority over other women as an enforcement and security unit, Khatiba Nusaybah was organized as a female military battalion. That distinction marked a further shift.</p>

<p>Women have also moved into specialized organizational functions beyond combat.</p>

<p>In January 2024 the <a href="https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy2056">Treasury Department designated</a> Egyptian national <a href="https://www.fbi.gov/wanted/terrorinfo/sarah-jamal-muhammad-al-sayyid">Sarah Jamal Muhammad al-Sayyid</a> for materially supporting the Islamic State group through her work with the Electronic Horizons Foundation, the group’s <a href="https://therecord.media/alleged-isis-cybersecurity-workers-sanctions-us-treasury">cybersecurity and operational security arm</a>. Treasury <a href="https://www.voanews.com/a/us-takes-shot-at-islamic-state-s-cyber-operations/7463815.html">says she recruited Islamic State members</a> into the organization, procured web servers for its platforms and helped with logistical management and cryptocurrency support.</p>

<p>Devorah Margolin, a terrorism researcher who specializes in women and gender in violent extremism, has <a href="https://extremism.gwu.edu/sites/g/files/zaxdzs5746/files/">shown how such groups</a> have expanded women’s roles to include financing and recruitment, often out of organizational necessity rather than principle.</p>

<p>Taken together, the Fluke-Ekren, Essa and al-Sayyid cases show women moving from auxiliary participation in jihadi groups into defined organizational functions carrying greater authority and responsibility.</p>

<p>The women who carry out violence have long been visible. Increasingly, so are the women who train recruits, enforce rules, supply doctrine and sustain the systems behind it.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292409/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Women are taking a more active role in jihadi organizations
Syria Deeply/https://deeply.thenewhumanitarian.org/syria Khadra Essa, a Somali-born Dutch citizen operating in Syria under the name Umm Qaqa al-Somali, is a wanted woman
State Department again publicized its offer of up to US$5 million for information about her whereabouts , having first offered a reward in April 2025

The notice describes Essa as the chief sharia instructor of Khatiba Nusaybah, or ISIS-NK, an all-female Islamic State combat battalion formed in Raqqa, Syria, in 2016 to recruit, organize and train female fighters
The United States alleges she received formal training in weapons, explosives and suicide operations

The State Department notice claims Essa “taught ISIS extremist ideology that justified suicide operations and killing of civilians,” recruited members, made orders that resulted in assaults and murder, and “led a group that violently enforced sharia law against women.” There is a separate State Department notice for information leading to the location and return of two American children allegedly taken by Essa after the death of their mother – an Islamic State group recruit – in 2019
Department of State has offered a $5 million reward for Khadra Essa

Department of State As a terrorism researcher who studies how militant groups organize and adapt, I’ve examined U.S. and European court records, sanctions and reward notices, as well as jihadi groups’ own Arabic-language publications, to trace how women’s roles inside armed movements have evolved
For as long as modern terrorism has existed, women have been known to fight and carry out attacks
But I’ve observed a newer development whereby women’s organizational authority in jihadi groups has been increasingly formalized
Indeed, women are occupying defined roles in which they train, recruit, discipline or direct other members, or manage functions on which the organization depends
Learning from secular groups Two decades ago, the political scientist Brigitte Nacos surveyed how women in armed groups were understood

Women had long been leaders and chief ideologues in secular movements – such as in the Weather Underground in the United States, Italy’s Red Brigades , Germany’s Red Army Faction and the Basque separatist group ETA
In jihadi movements, by contrast, women were rarely presented as people with formal authority over other members or organizational functions
Rather, such groups, exploiting the perception of women as less of a security threat , primarily saw women’s active role in offensive operations as that of a conveyor of bombs
It was a tactic that had already taken hold in secular militant movements

The Syrian Social Nationalist Party used Sana'a Mehaidli in a suicide attack in Lebanon in 1985; in 1991, a female Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam operative known as Dhanu assassinated Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi; and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party began deploying female bombers in the 1990s
By the early 2000s, Palestinian militant groups, including jihadists, were also using female suicide bombers
In January 2002, Wafa Idris died in Jerusalem while killing one man and wounding about 50 people
She is widely remembered as the first Palestinian woman to carry out a suicide bombing, although accounts indicate that the device may have detonated unexpectedly
Four more female suicide bombings followed within months of that attack
The Palestinian militant group Hamas initially resisted using women in suicide attacks but relented in 2004

Its spiritual leader, Ahmed Yassin, explained the change in tactical terms : “It could be that a man would not be able to reach the target, and that’s why they had to use a woman.” Beyond the bomber Within a few years, jihadi groups in Iraq , Jordan and Pakistan were also using female suicide bombers
But it was the Nigerian-based Boko Haram that has scaled the practice beyond any precedent
Research by the Combating Terrorism Center identified 434 bombers across 238 suicide attacks between April 2011 and June 2017 – at least 56% of them women
These cases largely placed women at the operational end of the process
Women carried the bomb or reached the target, but they were far less visible in positions that selected personnel, supplied doctrine, trained operatives or managed the organization itself
That conservative position initially guided groups such as al-Qaida

In December 2009, Umayma al-Zawahiri, wife of al-Qaida’s then deputy leader, published a “Letter to My Muslim Sisters.” It allowed women to fund operations, gather information and, in principle, carry out a suicide operation, while insisting their principal role was to raise fighters’ children, manage their homes and keep their secrets
But jihadi propaganda began to stretch the language used for women

In 2014, the Swahili-language magazine Al-Ghurabaa – aligned with al-Shabaab in Somalia – published an article titled “Mujahidah Leaders.” Translated and analyzed by Caleb Weiss , a researcher focused on jihadism in Africa, the magazine declared that “we sisters too have our own leaders.” It presented Aafia Siddiqui – a Pakistani neuroscientist convicted in 2010 of attempting to kill U.S. military and law enforcement personnel – and suspected mass murderer Samantha Lewthwaite as women to emulate
An Interpol ‘Red Notice’ for the arrest of terrorism suspect Samantha Lewthwaite on Sept. 26, 2013

Oli Scarff/Getty Images The rhetoric reflected a broader reality: Women in al-Shabaab had already served as recruiters, financiers, couriers and intelligence collectors, even if the movement rarely placed them in formal command positions
Expanding women’s roles The Islamic State group, meanwhile, was beginning to give some women a more concrete form of authority
In February 2014 it announced the formation of the all-female al-Khansaa Brigade in Syria

The unit emerged partly from a practical security problem: Men disguised in women’s clothing had carried out attacks against Islamic State group commanders, creating a need for women who could search women at checkpoints
Its responsibilities expanded into intelligence gathering, law enforcement, recruitment and policing other women
They could detain and punish other women, but their authority stopped there
The brigade occupied an “authoritative position” while remaining unable to challenge Islamic State group policy
That authority coexisted with a doctrine that still placed women primarily in the home

Roy will be the fourth case about Colorado antidiscrimination laws to wind up at the Supreme Court in 10 years.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/SupremeCourtTrumpElections/bb0cd2a929d84e4fb48100c34e0ec6c9/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=%22supreme%20court%22&amp;currentItemNo=45&amp;startingItemNo=50&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The U.S. Supreme Court <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/oral_arguments/2026TermCourtCalendar.pdf">begins its new term</a> on Oct. 5, 2026. One of the cases that the justices have agreed to hear is a First Amendment religious liberty case, <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/2026/25-581">St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy</a>.</p>

<p>The case arose because Colorado’s new <a href="https://cdec.colorado.gov/universal-preschool-colorado">Universal Preschool Program</a> only provides funding to preschools that agree to abide by a nondiscrimination policy. That policy forbids, among other things, denying admission because of a student’s or parent’s sexual orientation or gender identity.</p>

<p>Two Catholic parishes in the Archdiocese of Denver – St. Mary in Littleton and St. Bernadette in Lakewood – challenged that requirement and sued. They, along with Catholic parents who joined the lawsuit, argue that the nondiscrimination policy violated their First Amendment right to freely practice their religion.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://clasprofiles.wayne.edu/profile/hf1190">a constitutional law scholar</a> with <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/let-them-buy-cake-9780197853993?cc=us&amp;lang=en&amp;">a forthcoming book</a> about legal cases that pit First Amendment rights against LGBTQ rights, I consider St. Mary v. Roy to be significant for multiple reasons.</p>

<p>This case brings together major themes from recent Supreme Court cases about <a href="https://theconversation.com/are-religious-charter-schools-constitutional-after-deadlocked-scotus-decision-another-oklahoma-case-is-trying-to-find-out-292892">religion’s role in public life</a>, <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/24pdf/24-297_4f14.pdf">especially in education</a>. All these cases deal with <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-1/">the First Amendment</a>, which protects both freedom of speech and freedom of religion, along with several other rights.</p>

<p>But St. Mary is also significant for another, perhaps more surprising reason: It is yet another case from Colorado. </p>

<p>Throughout its history, the Supreme Court has considered less than a dozen cases that address, even tangentially, how to balance <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/22pdf/21-476_c185.pdf">free speech</a> or <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/24pdf/24-297_4f14.pdf">religious freedom</a> with <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/20pdf/19-123_g3bi.pdf">protections for the LGBTQ community</a>. Yet Colorado has been the source of <a href="https://www.coloradopolitics.com/2026/04/03/why-colorados-lgbtq-laws-keep-getting-struck-down-by-the-supreme-court/">five of these cases</a> over a 30-year period. </p>

<h2>Equal protection</h2>

<p>One of the earliest Supreme Court decisions recognizing constitutional protection for queer people was <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/1995/94-1039">Romer v. Evans</a>, a 1996 case from Colorado.</p>

<p>In the 1970s through the early 1990s, Colorado was a red-leaning state with several blue urban areas, like Aspen, Boulder and Denver. Many of these blue cities had passed <a href="https://aspen.gov/1698/Non-discrimination-ordinance">local ordinances against discrimination</a> based on sexual orientation in areas like housing and employment.</p>

<p>In the early 1990s, conservative groups <a href="https://repository.law.wisc.edu/s/uwlaw/media/329958">sought to nullify such ordinances</a> – including Focus on the Family, which had recently <a href="https://gazette.com/2017/03/27/focus-on-the-family-history-it-started-in-california-with-james-dobson-6a0af6e3-cac2-50fe-aa6b-8113da1d4684/">relocated its headquarters</a> to Colorado Springs. This coalition aimed to amend the state constitution to forbid any government entity from adopting or enforcing laws that prohibited discrimination against gay, lesbian or bisexual people. In 1992, <a href="https://www.cspm.org/cos-150-story/amendment-2/">a statewide ballot initiative</a> to approve such an amendment <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Amendment_2,_No_Protected_Status_for_Sexual_Orientation_Initiative_(1992)">passed with a roughly 53% majority</a>.</p>

<p>Several gay Coloradans and progressive municipalities, including Aspen, Boulder and Denver, sued. They argued that the new Colorado amendment violated the U.S. Constitution’s <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/amendment-14/">equal protection clause</a>, which requires that no state shall “deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws.”</p>

<p>Colorado defended the constitutionality of its new amendment by arguing that the goal was to show “respect for other citizens’ <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/amdt1-8-1/ALDE_00013139/">freedom of association</a>” – a right often defended on First Amendment grounds – especially for those “who have personal or religious objections to homosexuality.”</p>

<p>The case eventually made its way to the Supreme Court, which <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/1995/94-1039">sided with the gay plaintiffs and their allies</a> in a 6-3 decision. <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/517/620/">Writing for the majority</a>, Justice Anthony Kennedy concluded that “the amendment seems inexplicable by anything but animus toward the class that it affects”: gay, lesbian, and bisexual people. He concluded that the law lacked “a rational relationship to legitimate state interests” and thus was unconstitutional.</p>

<p>Romer v. Evans became the first U.S. Supreme Court decision to recognize equal protection rights for queer people.</p>

<h2>Role reversal</h2>

<p>In the 30 years since, there has been a stark role reversal. Colorado has become <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Presidential_voting_trends_in_Colorado">an increasingly blue state</a>. Meanwhile, the Supreme Court has gained a conservative supermajority with a record of siding with conservative religious litigants who argue that LGBTQ protections violate their First Amendment rights.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762908/original/file-20260929-50-jv9gz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="People in summer clothing, some of whom hold signs or brightly colored flags, walk down the middle of a broad street." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762908/original/file-20260929-50-jv9gz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762908/original/file-20260929-50-jv9gz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762908/original/file-20260929-50-jv9gz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762908/original/file-20260929-50-jv9gz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762908/original/file-20260929-50-jv9gz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762908/original/file-20260929-50-jv9gz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762908/original/file-20260929-50-jv9gz6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">People in a gay pride parade pass by the Colorado State Capitol in Denver on June 19, 2016.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/GayPrideEventsDenver/111d261608fe46a38e2f632a26528412/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=colorado%20%22state%20capitol%22%20pride&amp;currentItemNo=1&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Brennan Linsley</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>During the past decade, Colorado has defended its legal protections for queer people three times before the Supreme Court. Each time it has lost. </p>

<p>In the 2018 case, <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/2017/16-111">Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado</a>, a baker sued the state government, claiming that he had a free speech right and a religious free exercise right to refuse to provide a wedding cake for a same-sex couple. Both the Colorado Civil Rights Commission and the Colorado Court of Appeals ruled against the baker, on the grounds that such a refusal was sexual-orientation discrimination in violation of state law.</p>

<p>But <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/17pdf/16-111_j4el.pdf">in a 7-2 decision</a>, the Supreme Court vacated those rulings. Importantly, the majority did so on procedural grounds connected to a different issue. They left unanswered the underlying questions about how to balance the First Amendment with antidiscrimination law.</p>

<p>Five years later, the court heard a similar case where a web designer sought a right to <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/2022/21-476">refuse to make wedding websites for same-sex couples</a>. Unlike the baker, the designer had never been asked to provide services for a same-sex couple’s wedding. Instead, she proactively sued her home state, including the director of the Colorado Civil Rights Division, Aubrey Elenis, in her official capacity.</p>

<p>In a controversial 6-3 decision, <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/22pdf/21-476_c185.pdf">303 Creative v. Elenis</a>, the Supreme Court held that the designer had a free speech right to refuse to make wedding websites for same-sex couples. The majority opinion, however, did not acknowledge that doing so would amount to discrimination.</p>

<p>Finally, in March 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-539_fd9g.pdf">Chiles v. Salazar</a>, a case about whether Colorado’s ban on “conversion therapy,” which tries to change minors’ sexual orientation or gender identity, violated a therapist’s First Amendment rights. The Supreme Court did not address that underlying question; however, the justices did decide 8-1 that Colorado’s ban amounted to “viewpoint discrimination,” which occurs when a law regulates certain viewpoints but not others.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762910/original/file-20260929-50-gdba8o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A small group of women huddle with their arms around each other outside a tall building with marble columns." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762910/original/file-20260929-50-gdba8o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762910/original/file-20260929-50-gdba8o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762910/original/file-20260929-50-gdba8o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762910/original/file-20260929-50-gdba8o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762910/original/file-20260929-50-gdba8o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762910/original/file-20260929-50-gdba8o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762910/original/file-20260929-50-gdba8o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Members of ‘Concerned Women for America’ pray outside the Supreme Court building in Washington as justices hear arguments in Chiles v. Salazar, a case on ‘conversion therapy,’ in 2025.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/members-of-the-group-concerned-women-for-america-pray-news-photo/2239314750?adppopup=true">Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The justices sent the case back to a lower court for further deliberation. But <a href="https://firstamendment.mtsu.edu/article/viewpoint-discrimination/">viewpoint discrimination</a> is normally considered a violation of the First Amendment, which makes it likely that the medical providers advocating for a right to engage in conversion therapy would ultimately win their case.</p>

<p>The case <a href="https://www.thetrevorproject.org/blog/the-trevor-project-condemns-supreme-court-decision-to-treat-debunked-practice-of-conversion-therapy-as-protected-speech/">prompted an outcry</a> from queer people who have been harmed by the <a href="https://theconversation.com/conversion-therapy-is-discredited-and-increases-risk-of-suicide-yet-fewer-than-half-of-us-states-have-bans-in-place-161330">widely discredited practice</a>, as well as their allies and <a href="https://www.acslaw.org/expertforum/the-courts-conversion-therapy-decision-endangers-lgbtq-youth/">scholars of LGBTQ issues</a>.</p>

<h2>4th time in 10 years</h2>

<p>It is no coincidence that the plaintiffs challenging Colorado’s laws in all three cases were <a href="https://adflegal.org/article/colorado-vs-the-first-amendment-0-3-and-counting/">represented by attorneys from the same organization</a>: Alliance Defending Freedom, the country’s largest conservative Christian legal advocacy organization.</p>

<p>Alliance Defending Freedom has helped litigate <a href="https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2023/10/09/alliance-defending-freedoms-legal-crusade">many high-profile culture war cases</a>. Based in Arizona, the group has been active in taking on pro bono cases for conservative Christians who object to antidiscrimination protections for LGBTQ people in Colorado and elsewhere.</p>

<p>When oral arguments for St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy take place, Colorado will once again find itself defending its laws preventing discrimination against LGBTQ people in front of the high court. The court’s track record suggests it will likely face another uphill battle.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290122/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
