<title>3 iconic animals show the value of the US Endangered Species Act – and the harm in stripping it away</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762187/original/file-20260924-50-w6dr0e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=49%2C351%2C2177%2C1451&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A rescued Florida panther, one of fewer than 300 of the endangered big cats alive today, is released into the wild.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/myfwcmedia/8437968289">Mark Cunningham/Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>It <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/supct/html/94-859.ZO.html">used to be considered against the law</a> in America to starve a member of an endangered species to death or harm it by destroying its home. </p>

<p>That’s changing as the federal government chips away at the <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/16/chapter-35">U.S. Endangered Species Act</a>. Under the Trump administration’s <a href="https://www.sierraclub.org/sites/default/files/2026-09/fws-internal-memo-on-scope-of-esa-s-22take-22-prohibition.pdf">new interpretations of the law</a>, as long as <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/16/climate/endangered-species-act-change.html">the animal isn’t directly targeted</a>, there is no violation.</p>

<p>The new interpretations, <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-trumps-move-to-gut-the-endangered-species-act-likely-wont-hold-up-in-court-287671">if they hold up to court challenges</a>, could leave a vast number of endangered species at higher risk. Many of the country’s shipping, logging, mining and development practices are <a href="https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/topic/endangered-species-conservation/endangered-species-act-implementation">influenced by the Endangered Species Act</a>’s protections. In some cases, entire species <a href="https://theconversation.com/trumps-god-squad-pits-energy-vs-endangered-species-but-its-a-false-choice-protecting-wildlife-can-be-good-for-business-279433">could face extinction</a> if their habitats are no longer protected.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762188/original/file-20260924-58-qtajme.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="People in a rubber boat near the entangled whale. It's rostrum is visible above water near the equipment its tangled in." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762188/original/file-20260924-58-qtajme.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762188/original/file-20260924-58-qtajme.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=358&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762188/original/file-20260924-58-qtajme.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=358&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762188/original/file-20260924-58-qtajme.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=358&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762188/original/file-20260924-58-qtajme.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=449&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762188/original/file-20260924-58-qtajme.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=449&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762188/original/file-20260924-58-qtajme.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=449&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A Coast Guard cutter assists NOAA Fisheries and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission members in an attempt to free a North Atlantic right whale that became entangled in fishing gear. Fishing gear entanglements and vessel strikes are two of the biggest threats to these endangered whales.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:USCGC_Kingfisher_with_a_view_of_the_door_to_her_stern_launching_ramp.jpg">Alicia Windham-Reid</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As an <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=3_JsdOIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">environmental conservation scientist</a>, I have been following these and other changes affecting endangered species. To understand what they mean, let’s take a look at the potential impact on three very different species that are at risk: the Florida panther, the North Atlantic right whale and the monarch butterfly.</p>

<h2>What’s changing in how the law is carried out</h2>

<p>First, here’s what’s changing.</p>

<p>On Sept. 14, 2026, a Trump administration <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/14/2026-14195/rescinding-the-definition-of-harm-under-the-endangered-species-act">rule change went into effect</a> that <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-redefining-one-word-strips-the-endangered-species-acts-ability-to-protect-vital-habitat-287348">redefines harm</a> under the Endangered Species Act to mean only directly injuring or killing a member of an endangered species. The new definition removes an interpretation that had been used for half a century, and <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-trumps-move-to-gut-the-endangered-species-act-likely-wont-hold-up-in-court-287671">upheld by the Supreme Court</a>, that harming an endangered species includes eliminating that species’ habitat.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762189/original/file-20260924-58-851v63.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A stripped yellow and black caterpillar on a large fuzzy pod." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762189/original/file-20260924-58-851v63.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762189/original/file-20260924-58-851v63.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=403&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762189/original/file-20260924-58-851v63.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=403&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762189/original/file-20260924-58-851v63.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=403&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762189/original/file-20260924-58-851v63.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=507&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762189/original/file-20260924-58-851v63.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=507&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762189/original/file-20260924-58-851v63.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=507&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A monarch butterfly caterpillar crawls on a milkweed pod. Monarchs rely on milkweed for food and lay their eggs on the plants, but milkweed is also an aggressive weed in the Midwest.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Monarch_butterfly_caterpillar_insect_danaus_plexippus.jpg">Ron Singer/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>That move alone could gut the law’s ability to protect many species that face their biggest threat from losing habitat they rely on. </p>

<p>But that isn’t all. The director of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service <a href="https://www.sierraclub.org/sites/default/files/2026-09/fws-internal-memo-on-scope-of-esa-s-22take-22-prohibition.pdf">wrote a memo</a> to the services’ leadership team dated Sept. 14, 2026, further reinterpreting the law by arguing that it <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/16/climate/endangered-species-act-change.html">applies only to intentionally injuring or killing</a> an endangered species. So, if you didn’t target that animal, that would be OK. If your ship strikes a whale, or you kill endangered animals while building a new data center, that would no longer be a problem under this interpretation of the law unless you meant to kill the animal.</p>

<p>The administration also recently finalized its removal of what’s known as the <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/21/2026-14633/endangered-and-threatened-wildlife-and-plants-regulations-pertaining-to-endangered-and-threatened">Blanket 4(d) Rule</a>. That rule provided automatic protections for species listed as “threatened,” one step before they become “endangered,” and for their critical habitat.</p>

<p>As a result of these changes, species are still listed on paper as endangered but are largely unprotected.</p>

<h2>Florida panther: Territory loss and fragmentation</h2>

<p>The Florida panther (<em>Puma concolor coryi</em>) is a <a href="https://www.fws.gov/species/florida-panther-puma-concolor-coryi">majestic big cat</a> that stalks the state’s <a href="https://myfwc.com/wildlifehabitats/wildlife/panther/description/">southwestern pine forest and swamplands</a>, including the Everglades.</p>

<p>Its population crashed in the 1900s from overhunting, in part to protect livestock, and from habitat loss. The Florida panther was <a href="https://www.fws.gov/story/2022-04/florida-panther">close to extinction</a> when the <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/congress-passes-endangered-species-preservation-act/">Endangered Species Preservation Act of 1966</a>, the predecessor of the Endangered Species Act, was passed and led to changes that <a href="https://myfwc.com/media/29517/floridapantherssa_version1.pdf">began to help stabilize the population</a>. The state’s wildlife agencies believe the number of adult panthers today to be <a href="https://wildlifeflorida.org/florida-panthers/">between 120 and 230</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762190/original/file-20260924-60-3hc92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A big yellow cat under a tree stares into the camera." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762190/original/file-20260924-60-3hc92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762190/original/file-20260924-60-3hc92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=404&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762190/original/file-20260924-60-3hc92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=404&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762190/original/file-20260924-60-3hc92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=404&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762190/original/file-20260924-60-3hc92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=507&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762190/original/file-20260924-60-3hc92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=507&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762190/original/file-20260924-60-3hc92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=507&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Florida panthers are losing territory to development and face risks from road traffic. Only 120 to 230 of them remain.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Florida_panther(2)_(5164633462).jpg">Connie Bransilver/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Southeast Region</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>These top predators require <a href="https://www.nps.gov/teachers/classrooms/a-year-in-the-life-of-a-panther.htm">large home ranges</a> to live and hunt in, about 200 square miles (518 square kilometers) for males and 75 square miles (194 square kilometers) for females, so space is a scarce resource. And that’s where the challenge lies.</p>

<p>The public conservation areas are not capable of fully supporting the panther population. Roughly one-third of the panther’s main habitat is <a href="https://wildlifeflorida.org/how-one-florida-rancher-is-creating-space-for-panthers-to-thrive/">on private ranches and timberlands</a> that are frequently targeted for suburban development in southwestern Florida.</p>

<p><iframe id="l4X8z" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/l4X8z/3/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A chart shows the fall of the Florida panther population and slow rise again, but only about 150 Florida panthers remain in the wild today."></iframe></p>

<p>Under the new Endangered Species Act interpretations, it would <a href="https://law.stanford.edu/2026/07/23/endangered-species-acts-harm-rule-explained-what-the-change-means-for-wildlife/">not be considered a federal offense</a> to clear private palmetto flatwoods or cypress domes. Yet ecology research indicates that fragmenting habitat by breaking it up with roads and development results in panther deaths. The majority of panther deaths that aren’t natural are <a href="https://myfwc.com/wildlifehabitats/wildlife/panther/biology/">due to collisions with vehicles</a> as they attempt to cross busy roads.</p>



<p>The revised rule also allows landowners to clear areas that had been preserved as wildlife corridors on their land without being liable for harming the panthers. That could accelerate <a href="https://www.fws.gov/story/2022-04/florida-panther">habitat loss in southwest Florida’s Caloosahatchee River basin</a> and undermine many years of effort put into the <a href="https://theconversation.com/florida-panthers-and-black-bears-need-a-literal-path-for-survival-heres-how-the-florida-wildlife-corridor-provides-it-in-one-of-the-fastest-growing-us-states-251790">Florida Wildlife Corridor</a>, a connected network of public and private lands that allow the Florida panther and other species to roam.</p>

<h2>North Atlantic right whale: Noisy, dangerous seas</h2>

<p>In the ocean, habitat is influenced not only by the water but also by sounds that travel through it. That’s particularly true for whale habitat.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/species/north-atlantic-right-whale">North Atlantic right whale</a> (<em>Eubalaena glacialis</em>) is one of the most endangered whale species, with an estimated population of about <a href="https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/national/endangered-species-conservation/north-atlantic-right-whale-calving-season-2026">380 animals and only around 70 breeding females</a> remaining, primarily along the North American Atlantic coast.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762191/original/file-20260924-60-gdni0p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A right whale and its calf" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762191/original/file-20260924-60-gdni0p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762191/original/file-20260924-60-gdni0p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762191/original/file-20260924-60-gdni0p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762191/original/file-20260924-60-gdni0p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762191/original/file-20260924-60-gdni0p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762191/original/file-20260924-60-gdni0p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762191/original/file-20260924-60-gdni0p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">North Atlantic right whales rely on sound traveling long distances through water to communicate. That communication gets harder as the ocean becomes noisier.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:SBNMS_-right_whale_(27907275651).jpg">NOAA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Right whales communicate with <a href="https://dosits.org/galleries/audio-gallery/marine-mammals/baleen-whales/north-atlantic-right-whale/">low-frequency sounds</a> that help them navigate, locate food and connect with their calves. </p>

<p>The noise caused by ships, seismic surveys used in oil exploration, and pile-driving associated with offshore energy projects <a href="https://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/science/sentinel-site-program/monterey-bay/noise.html">results in background noise</a> that can disrupt these signals. </p>

<p><iframe id="5ZIrl" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/5ZIrl/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="The North Atlantic right whale, among the most endangered whales, began a recovery in the second half of the 20th century, but its numbers fell again with increasing ocean activity in the 21st century."></iframe></p>

<p>In addition to sound interference, whales face physical risks from being struck by boats and becoming entangled in fishing gear. The new interpretations of the Endangered Species Act remove some of the legal basis for enforcing rules for noisy seismic surveys, speed limits on vessels and restrictions on shipping routes designed to help protect the whales from harm.</p>

<h2>Monarch butterfly: Living in a regulatory limbo</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://www.fws.gov/species/monarch-danaus-plexippus">eastern migratory monarch butterfly</a> (<em>Danaus plexippus</em>), a delicate orange-and-black butterfly that was once plentiful across North America’s prairies in summer, is an example of a species that would benefit from the <a href="https://earthjustice.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/2026-07-21-60-day-letter-on-4d-rule-final-pdf.pdf">Blanket 4(d) Rule</a>.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.umesc.usgs.gov/management/dss/monarch.html">butterfly’s population has fallen by about 80%</a> over the past decade, largely due to habitat loss. In the U.S., that includes the <a href="https://www.usgs.gov/news/national-news-release/billions-more-milkweeds-needed-restore-monarchs">loss of milkweed</a>, which the butterflies <a href="https://coastalbg.uga.edu/2023/10/the-connection-between-milkweed-and-monarch-butterflies/">rely on for food and laying eggs</a> as they travel through the Midwest, but that can compete with crops.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762192/original/file-20260924-50-yrs1dm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An orange and black butterfly on a pink constellation of tiny flowers." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762192/original/file-20260924-50-yrs1dm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762192/original/file-20260924-50-yrs1dm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=379&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762192/original/file-20260924-50-yrs1dm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=379&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762192/original/file-20260924-50-yrs1dm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=379&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762192/original/file-20260924-50-yrs1dm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=477&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762192/original/file-20260924-50-yrs1dm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=477&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762192/original/file-20260924-50-yrs1dm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=477&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3d/Monarch_butterfly_swamp_milkweed_Michigan_15_August_2016.png?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=index&amp;utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled">Jim Hudgins/USFWS</a></span>

<p>In the past, whenever a species was <a href="https://www.fws.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ESA-Section-4-Listing.pdf">listed as threatened</a> – a step below endangered, and the status being <a href="https://www.fws.gov/our-work/pollinators/save-monarch">recommended for the monarch butterfly</a> – it automatically received protections under the Blanket 4(d) Rule. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/21/2026-14633/endangered-and-threatened-wildlife-and-plants-regulations-pertaining-to-endangered-and-threatened">Without that rule</a>, threatened species no longer get automatic protections and instead rely on agencies drawing up species-specific rules for each one, a process that can take years.</p>

<h2>Losing proactive protection</h2>

<p>The reinterpretations of the Endangered Species Act change the law from one that is proactive to one that takes action only after there has been immediate and intentional physical harm.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762210/original/file-20260925-50-r70ajq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A whale sticking its nose up above the water." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762210/original/file-20260925-50-r70ajq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762210/original/file-20260925-50-r70ajq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762210/original/file-20260925-50-r70ajq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762210/original/file-20260925-50-r70ajq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762210/original/file-20260925-50-r70ajq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762210/original/file-20260925-50-r70ajq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762210/original/file-20260925-50-r70ajq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">A North American right whale sticks its rostrum – its jaw and snout – above the water.</span>

            </figcaption>

<p>Hunting is not the primary threat today to the Florida panther, the North Atlantic right whale or the monarch butterfly. Their survival instead relies on the pine flatwoods being in good health, the ocean remaining quiet, and milkweed corridors existing across the continent.</p>

<p>Since nature does not abide by the legal boundaries between species and their habitats, damaging the habitat can result in the loss of the species.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292887/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: A rescued Florida panther, one of fewer than 300 of the endangered big cats alive today, is released into the wild

Mark Cunningham/Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission , CC BY-SA It used to be considered against the law in America to starve a member of an endangered species to death or harm it by destroying its home
That’s changing as the federal government chips away at the U.S
Under the Trump administration’s new interpretations of the law , as long as the animal isn’t directly targeted , there is no violation
The new interpretations, if they hold up to court challenges , could leave a vast number of endangered species at higher risk
Many of the country’s shipping, logging, mining and development practices are influenced by the Endangered Species Act ’s protections
In some cases, entire species could face extinction if their habitats are no longer protected
A Coast Guard cutter assists NOAA Fisheries and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission members in an attempt to free a North Atlantic right whale that became entangled in fishing gear
Fishing gear entanglements and vessel strikes are two of the biggest threats to these endangered whales
Alicia Windham-Reid As an environmental conservation scientist , I have been following these and other changes affecting endangered species
To understand what they mean, let’s take a look at the potential impact on three very different species that are at risk: the Florida panther, the North Atlantic right whale and the monarch butterfly
What’s changing in how the law is carried out First, here’s what’s changing
On Sept. 14, 2026, a Trump administration rule change went into effect that redefines harm under the Endangered Species Act to mean only directly injuring or killing a member of an endangered species
The new definition removes an interpretation that had been used for half a century, and upheld by the Supreme Court , that harming an endangered species includes eliminating that species’ habitat
A monarch butterfly caterpillar crawls on a milkweed pod
Monarchs rely on milkweed for food and lay their eggs on the plants, but milkweed is also an aggressive weed in the Midwest
Fish and Wildlife Service That move alone could gut the law’s ability to protect many species that face their biggest threat from losing habitat they rely on

Fish and Wildlife Service wrote a memo to the services’ leadership team dated Sept. 14, 2026, further reinterpreting the law by arguing that it applies only to intentionally injuring or killing an endangered species
So, if you didn’t target that animal, that would be OK

If your ship strikes a whale, or you kill endangered animals while building a new data center, that would no longer be a problem under this interpretation of the law unless you meant to kill the animal
The administration also recently finalized its removal of what’s known as the Blanket 4(d) Rule
That rule provided automatic protections for species listed as “threatened,” one step before they become “endangered,” and for their critical habitat
As a result of these changes, species are still listed on paper as endangered but are largely unprotected

Florida panther: Territory loss and fragmentation The Florida panther ( Puma concolor coryi ) is a majestic big cat that stalks the state’s southwestern pine forest and swamplands , including the Everglades
Its population crashed in the 1900s from overhunting, in part to protect livestock, and from habitat loss

The Florida panther was close to extinction when the Endangered Species Preservation Act of 1966 , the predecessor of the Endangered Species Act, was passed and led to changes that began to help stabilize the population
The state’s wildlife agencies believe the number of adult panthers today to be between 120 and 230
Florida panthers are losing territory to development and face risks from road traffic

Fish and Wildlife Service Southeast Region , CC BY These top predators require large home ranges to live and hunt in, about 200 square miles (518 square kilometers) for males and 75 square miles (194 square kilometers) for females, so space is a scarce resource
The public conservation areas are not capable of fully supporting the panther population
Roughly one-third of the panther’s main habitat is on private ranches and timberlands that are frequently targeted for suburban development in southwestern Florida
Under the new Endangered Species Act interpretations, it would not be considered a federal offense to clear private palmetto flatwoods or cypress domes
Yet ecology research indicates that fragmenting habitat by breaking it up with roads and development results in panther deaths
The majority of panther deaths that aren’t natural are due to collisions with vehicles as they attempt to cross busy roads
The revised rule also allows landowners to clear areas that had been preserved as wildlife corridors on their land without being liable for harming the panthers

That could accelerate habitat loss in southwest Florida’s Caloosahatchee River basin and undermine many years of effort put into the Florida Wildlife Corridor , a connected network of public and private lands that allow the Florida panther and other species to roam
North Atlantic right whale: Noisy, dangerous seas In the ocean, habitat is influenced not only by the water but also by sounds that travel through it
That’s particularly true for whale habitat

The North Atlantic right whale ( Eubalaena glacialis ) is one of the most endangered whale species, with an estimated population of about 380 animals and only around 70 breeding females remaining, primarily along the North American Atlantic coast
North Atlantic right whales rely on sound traveling long distances through water to communicate

title: Trump’s “Most EXCLUSIVE DINNER IN THE WORLD”
excerpt: Donald Trump waves to the media on the South Lawn of the White House on September 26, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logof
body: Donald Trump waves to the media on the South Lawn of the White House on September 26, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is once again selling access to the highest bidder(s).  What’s happening? On Thursday, the Washington Sun’s Jeff Stein reported that Trump will reprise his 2025 “crypto dinner” later this year, hosting some of the top investors in the $TRUMP memecoin at his Virginia golf club.  The top 185 holders of $TRUMP will receive an invite to the event, which the website describes as the “Most EXCLUSIVE DINNER IN THE WORLD.” The top 29 $TRUMP holders will also be eligible for a “special VIP reception.”  What is $TRUMP? As my colleague Adam Clark Estes explained last year , memecoins like $TRUMP are “all but make-believe.” The coin is a crypto token, or “a type of digital asset that’s built on a cryptocurrency’s blockchain, but it is not a full featured cryptocurrency, like bitcoin.”  In other words, buying it doesn’t get you very much — the value of the coin has collapsed since early last year when Trump took office — but it will get you a chance to have dinner with the president.  What’s the context? This will be the third major event Trump has hosted for buyers of $TRUMP, following a May 2025 dinner at his Virginia club and a “crypto and business conference” earlier this year at Mar-a-Lago , where Trump gave a keynote speech.  But it’s just one of the many, many ways that Trump and his family have found to enrich themselves through crypto: There’s also another memecoin, $MELANIA, and his lucrative crypto firm, World Liberty Financial, which received a $500 million investment from a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family last year

Strictly speaking, as Stein points out, Trump himself does not own the company minting $TRUMP, though he still profits handsomely , to the tune of $636 million last year, from transaction fees and other revenue
And he’s made even more off World Liberty Financial, which he and his sons do own, along with others: $799 million in 2025 alone, according to financial disclosure forms filed earlier this year

And with that, it’s time to log off… Don’t miss this story about “junk journaling” from my colleague Rachel Miller, a hobby that she describes as “a great way to cope with digital malaise and existential dread.” (Needed!) You can read it with a gift link here
Plus: It’s a big day for Denali National Park’s sled dog puppies, of whom I’m a big fan.

title: How both parties have changed since 2024
excerpt: People cast ballots on the second day of early voting in Wheaton, Illinois, on September 25, 2026. | Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared
body: People cast ballots on the second day of early voting in Wheaton, Illinois, on September 25, 2026. | Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day
Depending on your political appetite and your geographic location, you absolutely do not need me to remind you of the upcoming midterm elections

But for those of you unencumbered by an unhealthy attachment to political news, and unassaulted by the onslaught of ever-more-brazen political ads , consider this your official notice that the midterms are approaching
In less than six weeks, Americans will head to the polls to decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices

The stakes are arguably unusually high: Voters will choose whether to check the power of a president who has bulldozed over historical norms and limits.  So starting this evening, I’m partnering with my colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s Midterms, Actually team for five weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the 2026 midterms
Together with outside experts, we’ll break down one issue each week and suggest further reading and races to watch in November
Up first, and without further ado: the profound shift that both parties have experienced since the 2024 election

Go a little deeper View Link To kick this series off, I asked Astead to imagine a hypothetical world in which he hadn’t followed politics since 2024. (An outlandish counterfactual: Astead is acutely plugged into politics.) But in this alternate universe, I asked, what would surprise him most about 2026? Easy, he said
The GOP’s disillusionment with President Donald Trump, who remade the party in his image.  Let’s put some numbers on that phenomenon, to start
Trump’s approval rating has dipped to record lows, even among Republicans
According to an NBC poll conducted in mid-September, just four in 10 Republicans strongly approve of Trump’s performance, down 11 percentage points from the spring
Republicans have soured on Trump over his handling of the economy and attacks on Iran, which violated his promise to keep America out of foreign wars

Trump’s delayed release of the Epstein files also fueled distrust in his base by exposing his own ties to the dreaded “elite insiders.” In response, some Republican candidates have worked to distance themselves from Trump , even defying him in campaign ads
But it’s unclear whether that tactic will win over disillusioned or disengaged Republicans
If enough stay home, Astead said — especially with Democrats eager to vote — Democrats could flip the House and/or Senate and make Trump’s last years in office far more difficult
And speaking of Democrats…they’re  also undergoing a major transformation after their 2024 presidential defeat
That loss disproved their previous theory of Trump-era politics: namely, that Trump’s rise was an aberration that competence, decency, and normalcy would eventually overcome

By contrast, today’s Democrats want a party that “fights,” Astead told me. “The open question is who they’re fighting: The oligarchy? Big Tech? The Billionaire/Epstein class? Trump’s Republican Party?”  Democrats face ideological questions, too
Since 2024, voters have lost trust in the establishment and in party leaders’ ability to pick the best candidates; left-wing candidates have thrived in that vacuum
It’s pretty wild, when you think about it, that a Muslim democratic socialist in New York ranks among America’s most popular Democrats
For both parties, then, November 3 is a test of their respective visions for America
Not just between the parties — as in, Republicans vs
That, in turn, will help determine the rest of Trump’s presidency…and the 2028 presidential election.  But it’s only October 1

Let’s not get ahead of ourselves.  ➨ Races to watch: Michigan’s Senate race , where progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers; Florida’s 27th District, where Republican María Elvira Salazar publicly broke with Trump ; and the Nebraska, Idaho, and South Dakota’s Senate races , where independent candidates will test both sides’ exhaustion with the two-party system. ➨  More from Vox:  It’s not the left rising
Is it too little, too late? What Democrats are still getting wrong about voters One link for later ➨ “Decant” your berries and asparagus
They’ll last longer with more space and air

title: Disney World solved a problem that could save America billions every year
excerpt: How to untangle our underground mess of cables, gas lines, and pipes. | Bing Guan/Bloomberg via Getty Images Buried beneath every American city is a mysterious
body: How to untangle our underground mess of cables, gas lines, and pipes. | Bing Guan/Bloomberg via Getty Images Buried beneath every American city is a mysterious jumble of cables, pipes, and gas lines, entangled like a pair of wired headphones the moment you pull them out of your pocket

Every time a contractor sticks a shovel in the asphalt, they embark on a high-risk excavate-by-dots obstacle course, dodging color-coded clusters of spaghetti-like power lines, gas mains, sewers, and fiber-optic cables

Orange is telecom.  About 700,000 times a year — that’s once every 47 seconds — something goes wrong.  A backhoe slices into a cable and cuts off a 911 call center , or a woman comes home to find her dryer and hot water heater on fire after a contractor pierced her electrical line

Just last week, a contractor accidentally severed a single telecommunication cable that proved critical enough to ground flights at some of the nation’s largest airports on the eve of the UN General Assembly, ensnaring even world leaders like Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in delays .  The ground beneath our city streets has never been so crowded, driven by a furious race to lay fiber optic cables carrying the data that fills your social media feeds and transmits your ChatGPT queries

Nor have the systems we use to find out where it’s safe to dig — namely, a hotline and all that colorful spray paint — ever felt so catastrophically insufficient.  “If the locator mismarked the line, if the line wasn’t marked, if there was no map that even said the line was there,” said Sarah Magruder Lyle, president of the Common Ground Alliance, a trade association focused on underground damage prevention, “there are a variety of issues that could happen before the excavator even puts a shovel or a backhoe in the ground.” According to Common Ground, such incidents cost the US about $83.2 billion per year , roughly as much as we invest in public transit annually nationwide

But the actual financial toll may be even higher, because every time a crew stumbles across a mislabeled power line or a gas pipe everyone else forgot about, it can delay construction for months on end
As Magruder Lyle put it, “if they get out there and they find something that they’re not supposed to, you have to go back and reengineer the whole project.”  Such surprises can also lead to tragedy

A 5-year-old named Alistair Lamb was killed in Missouri last spring after a contractor drilled into a gas line near his home, spewing fumes that leveled his house when his unsuspecting father flipped a light switch
And just this May, another unmarked gas line killed three people when contractors struck it, leading an apartment complex in Dallas to explode

Yet the messy underbelly of our cities remains largely invisible, with accountability for issues foisted upon and at times evaded by a hodgepodge of finger-pointing private utility companies, agencies, and contractors

And that’s a shame because there is, in fact, a better way to bury the cables and pipelines that our modern lives depend on, and a multitude of better ways that we can find the ones we’ve already buried.  What Disney World gets right about the stuff we bury To understand one utopian vision for how all this could work, look no further than the happiest place on Earth
That’s a moniker Disney World has earned, in my mind, not for its Mickey Mouse waffles (though my niece may disagree), but for its world-class utility corridors, also known as utilidors
Directly beneath the Magic Kingdom is a sprawling network of tunnels
Initially designed to shepherd around Mickey and his friends, the system now also serves as one of the largest utility corridors ever created

Unlike the rest of America, where cables are typically dumped in ditches before being covered with dirt, the electrical lines that power Cinderella’s castle quite literally get the princess treatment.  Alongside water pipes, sewers, and animatronic control systems, these power lines lace the walls and ceilings of the utilidors, meaning they’re protected from weather and changes in the soil
They are also easy to monitor, catalog, and access if something needs fixing

While the cost of building a controlled system like this is much higher upfront than burying directly in the ground, the practice virtually eliminates the risk of accidentally rupturing a gas main or slicing a fiber optic cable during routine maintenance

Once they’re built, they can also drastically reduce costs in the long run because you no longer need to tear up a street every time a utility needs fixing.  “Obviously, it’s expensive,” said Debra Laefer, a professor of civil and urban engineering at New York University, “but in the long term, it would be hugely cheaper,” especially “in areas where we are digging all the time, there’s a direct business case for moving towards these utilidors.” As fantastical as Disney World’s imagineered system may seem — and it was, to be clear, predicated on a not-easily-reproducible master plan — the idea of storing utility lines in easy-to-access tunnels is not just for amusement parks

It is possible even in places where most of those lines are currently lying in the dirt, as Prague proved back in the 1970s, when the city decided it was fed up with destroying its precious cobblestone streets every time a buried pipe or cable needed fixing

The city now boasts a sprawling utility tunnel network, occasionally patrolled, evidently, by a couple of robot dogs tasked with mapping out every cable.  Singapore has also spent years building out walkable utility corridors that operate much like the Magic Kingdom’s, transmitting water, data, and energy from the safety of well-organized underground tunnels

Some of Tokyo’s largest districts store their cables and gas lines in huge concrete utility ducts , and many Parisian water lines and fiber optics are kept across the city’s centuries-old sewer system, a catacombs of waste made easily navigable by blue-and-white street signs that correspond to the avenues above
Many university campuses across the US also boast their own sprawling utilidors
In most cases, cities chose not to relocate utilities all at once, a feat that would probably be financially prohibitive and deeply disruptive

Rather, they took advantage of all the times they’ve needed to relocate utility lines anyway, a standard (and expensive) practice for big building projects like the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing or the Second Avenue Subway, a major transportation project in New York City that’s been consistently delayed by unmapped utility lines

A group of graduate students found that building such a tunnel in parts of NYC would likely cost at least twice as much as dropping a utility line in the ground, but could recoup the costs within 47 years.  “There are streets in New York City that have been excavated at least once a year, every year for the past 30 years,” Laefer said

If you just prioritize those streets, gathering the piping in a “big concrete box” underground, you could allow workers to complete most repairs without needing to disturb the streets or sidewalks above at all

But building new utility tunnels would require that we first come to better understand the wires and piping already entangled under our cities, which if you recall, we have only a surprisingly flimsy picture of in most cities today
But if every surprise utility line is an opportunity to move it somewhere better, it is also an opportunity, at the very least, to map out where it is

To that end, a few years ago, Laefer led a $1.2 million pilot funded by the National Science Foundation to create a test case for 3D-mapping New York City’s underground utilities, a project that’s since been adopted into a citywide initiative
The city says it plans to roll out the spruced up utilities locating system in 2028
The UK debuted a similar digital map of over 3 million kilometers of underground pipes and power, owned by hundreds of utilities and agencies a few years ago
The nation projects that it could help save over $500 million per year by minimizing delays and accidental damage

In places where Singapore has not yet stuffed its utilities into walkable tunnels, the city’s own mapping and utilities coordination has already saved it an estimated $230 million in avoided clashes since 2024
Not bad for an intervention that doesn’t even require any physical rebuilding

So why hasn’t every American city copied London or Singapore? Well, US cities tend to be plagued by even more private utilities and patchwork local and state norms and regulations than a nation like the United Kingdom
Getting them to pool together what they often consider proprietary underground data is challenging, and few local officials have opted to prioritize such efforts

But this may well change as more and more fiber optics go into the ground, more flights get canceled, more apartment complexes explode , more power lines flicker off , more sinkholes form , and more Americans come to be all too acquainted with the perils lurking just beneath our feet.  “I think at this point, it’s more about political will and money than any technical obstacle,” Laefer said. “Technically, we’re there

title: The Democrats who bet wrong on ICE
excerpt: Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming across the 2026 primaries, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground
body: Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming across the 2026 primaries, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground
You can sign up here to get it in your inbox every week
One big idea: Democrats’ Laken Riley vote is aging badly Two things happened this week that reveal how quickly the politics of immigration enforcement are shifting

Jim Justice of West Virginia, a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, urged the administration to dial back its enforcement push . “Before you know it, you get people that get carried away in their job and whatever it may be, and all of a sudden, then you’re dragging people away that have lived on your street corner for 15 years,” Justice told Politico this week. “I don’t know that we need to be doing that stuff.” And he’s not the only red-state Republican who’s been pushing back on ICE lately, including some facing voters in tough races next month
The second thing flew under the radar: Sen

Jon Ossoff, the Georgia Democrat running for reelection who has also been floated as a 2028 presidential candidate , struggled to explain himself when a reporter confronted him on camera about his vote for the Laken Riley Act in January 2025

Passed within days of Trump’s inauguration and signed nine days into his second term, the law requires ICE to detain undocumented immigrants who are merely arrested for or charged with theft-related crimes, before any conviction

In the exchange with a reporter from Drop Site News, Ossoff talked about his Senate work investigating alleged ICE abuses, but didn’t directly address his vote after being asked if he regretted it. “Laken Riley was my constituent and what happened to her should happen to no American, to no person in this world,” Ossoff said. “I think that immigration enforcement should be focused on those who are convicted or charged with serious crimes.” He excused himself to walk into a meeting as the reporter pressed him on whether the law undermined due process.  In both cases, you see changing winds of electoral politics

Back in 2025, when Ossoff and 11 other Senate Democrats joined Republicans in supporting Trump’s immigration bill, they implicitly validated Trump’s premise on immigration enforcement: that not only was the border out of control, but that there also needed to be new efforts to step up interior enforcement through expanding agencies like ICE

In the year-plus since that vote, Trump has hired more ICE officers, launched sweeping raids in cities like Minneapolis, Chicago, and Los Angeles, and fueled a cauldron of chaos that’s led to shootings across the country
Politically, it has now put Democrats like Ossoff in a pickle, one that will matter more the closer we get to 2028

How do you explain giving more immigration powers to a Stephen Miller-led White House? How can one argue you couldn’t have seen this coming? In some ways, you can understand the political logic of the time

Ossoff, who is running in a state Trump carried, and many of the congressional Democrats who supported the Laken Riley law were in competitive races, and Democrats left the 2024 election thinking they had misread the electorate on the issue, particularly after Latino voters swung hard toward the right

But given what’s happened since, it’s clear many congressional Democrats made a familiar mistake: prioritizing political triangulation over standing on their values of protecting marginalized communities
Take a look at some of the Democrats who have already had to walk back their votes
In the Democratic primary for Minnesota’s open Senate seat, Lt

Angie Craig’s vote for the law a key focus of her campaign , calling it “disqualifying.” The attacks were so effective that Craig eventually expressed remorse, saying, “I wanted to be honest with the people of Minnesota
I will tell you when I get it wrong, and I got that one wrong.” Craig lost the August 11 primary to Flanagan
Maryland’s April McClain Delaney, another congressional Democrat, also said she regretted her vote: “I will say that this was in the beginning of my term

And I never thought that ICE immigration and the horror of what has happened would happen.” (She survived her primary, defeating David Trone by 6 points .) It’s easy to see where the buyer’s remorse is emanating from

And as we’ve talked about on this Substack and in our reporting on America, Actually , Trump is doing worse and worse with Latino voters, with both prices and immigration enforcement driving the slide

A Hart Research poll for TelevisaUnivision of 1,500 Latino registered voters in battleground House districts (August 6–17) found 63 percent disapprove of Trump’s job performance and 62 percent disapprove of his handling of immigration enforcement and deportations

Sixty-four percent view ICE unfavorably.  When I recently talked to Stephanie Valencia of Equis Research, she said this:  The people who feel most regretful who voted for Trump in 2024 are most regretful because of immigration
They feel like there was a broken promise there

Like, they were told he was gonna focus on the border, which everybody agreed was chaos, and he was gonna focus on violent criminals and serious threats, and at the end of the day, he has not complied with that
But while the shift in public opinion helps explain the elected officials’ political logic, it doesn’t change the material harm of their votes
Just this week, ICE announced plans to hire 5,000 more employees , most of them deportation officers, by the end of the year as enforcement continues to ramp up
And these raids have a lasting effect on targeted communities, like in Maine, the Chicago area, and Texas
It’s the No. 1 issue that has come up in my conversations with local reporters
The chief architect of this chaos is the president, but make no mistake: Trump had help from shortsighted Democrats

One thing I’m hearing  Maya Miller is a Report for America corps member covering democracy and government for the Gulf States Newsroom, a public radio collaboration that includes Louisiana’s WWNO and WRKF
She’s been reporting on Mississippi’s redistricting fight and what residents are saying about their representation and the upcoming midterms
You’ve been reporting from redistricting hearings in Mississippi
What are residents most concerned about, and is there a conversation or moment that captures the mood? Residents are most concerned about their representation
In Mississippi in particular, race and party are strongly intertwined, and Black residents worry that by being drawn into new districts, voters may elect a Republican candidate
There was a bit of secrecy around redistricting earlier this summer, with Gov
Tate Reeves, a Republican, canceling a special session to redraw judicial lines
So advocates created the People’s Hearings, a series of meetings held across the state to voice concerns and create a public record of testimonies from Mississippians

Quickly after, lawmakers decided to host their own public hearings, and at these hearings, hundreds of residents showed up, mostly to urge them not to redistrict. “It seems to me that the threat of losing representation has made people more aware of the moving parts.” At one hearing, I spoke to Joyce Arceneaux-Mathis, president of the Natchez NAACP
She’s frustrated that the state is going to spend millions on new maps when people are struggling with day to day expenses

title: “We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer
excerpt: Still putting out fires: Two months after OpenAI's agents hacked Hugging Face, new incidents keep surfacing—including a breach of Australia's national
body: Still putting out fires: Two months after OpenAI's agents hacked Hugging Face, new incidents keep surfacing—including a breach of Australia's national health system that wasn't disclosed for 84 days
OpenAI has since paused model training until it can put stronger safeguards in place
The monitors weren't on: OpenAI's chief research officer Mark Chen admits the company wasn't watching its models during training—only after deployment
That gap let early warning signs, like agents casually reaching out on Slack for help, go from amusing quirks to serious security failures

A calculated slowdown, not a retreat: Chen says OpenAI has shifted 5–10% of its computing power toward safety and monitoring, but insists it won't fall so far behind competitors that it loses influence over industry norms—calling that "a horrible strategy." A darker forecast ahead: Chen dropped his optimism when asked about open-source models, warning that within six to twelve months, the world could see deliberately misaligned agents—built to attack infrastructure—beyond the reach of any regulation. " data-chronoton-post-id="1145339" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Two months after the bombshell news that a swarm of its agents had broken their containment and hacked into the computers of the AI company Hugging Face , OpenAI is still putting out fires
A steady drip of disclosures about other hacks in the weeks since has kept OpenAI in the spotlight and raised serious questions about the safety of its technology
Last week brought news of another hack, this time into Australia’s national health-care system
The Australian government says that OpenAI did not notify it of the breach until 84 days after it happened

But OpenAI insists it is not on the back foot. “I do kind of reject the premise that OpenAI is a company with visible impacts in the world and therefore OpenAI is not training safe and aligned models,” says Mark Chen, the company’s chief research officer
The recent agent hacks were accidents that happened during the testing of experimental models on his watch

In a lot of ways, the buck stops with him.  I sat down with Chen in London last Friday to talk about the fallout from the hacks, what his company is doing about it, and why he thinks things are not as bad as they seem

Later that same day, OpenAI put out a report detailing yet another incident —the first since the company says it took measures to prevent them—in which its agents once again broke out and accessed the public internet when they were not meant to
Over the weekend, OpenAI announced that it had paused the training of its latest models
A company spokesperson says: “We will resume only when we’re confident we have additional safeguards and alignments in place

This is not the first time we’ve paused to take such measures, nor do we expect it to be the last as AI capabilities continue to advance.” OpenAI also says that it is now reviewing logs of agent activity dating back to January 2026 to understand what happened in these hacks
The way Chen sees it, the Hugging Face incident triggered a welcome course correction for the industry
And he wants you to know that OpenAI is setting an example he hopes other companies will follow. “If you disappeared OpenAI, that would be bad for the world,” he says

Out of control Chen claims that the drumbeat of new cases in which OpenAI has lost control of its models reflects a deliberate choice on the company’s part. “When it comes to the broader sphere of effects of the Hugging Face incident, this is something that we have been aware of and we’re figuring out the process of disclosure,” he says. “We want to make sure we do in-depth investigations before we just put details out there in the open.” The trouble with this approach is that it gives the impression OpenAI has an ongoing problem that it is failing to fix

He says the multiple cases (that we know of so far) in which his company’s agents broke containment and behaved in unexpected and undesirable ways were all part of the same cluster of activity in May and June that led to the Hugging Face hack

In short, you can blame the same few models running under the same flawed testing procedures—models and procedures that OpenAI has since dropped, Chen says.     “It’s not like, you know, Hugging Face happened and we patched that and then something else happened and we patched that,” he adds. “We’re just kind of making sure that we responsibly disclose the full waterfall of what happened.” At least that was the case before Friday’s announcement that OpenAI’s agents had been caught accessing the internet on September 20, weeks after the company claims to have set up new safeguards

In its defense, OpenAI says the activity was flagged 15 minutes after it started (it took the company more than a week to notice the Hugging Face hack) and that this shows the new systems it has put in place to spot such activity are working

What’s changed I want to understand what’s changed inside OpenAI in the aftermath of this summer’s hacks that makes Chen confident his team is now back in control. “Hugging Face felt like a very serious thing,” he says. “There are so many novel behaviors right there
There were multiple agents collaborating on a message board; they found their way out of OpenAI’s infrastructure

We don’t want this kind of thing to ever happen again.” The realization for OpenAI, says Chen, was that models need to be watched while they are still being trained, not only once they are deployed: “From that moment on, we have treated the process of training as something that’s not secure,” he says
OpenAI, like other top AI firms, has systems in place to monitor the behavior of its models
It uses specialized LLMs to monitor its consumer models, keeping tabs on their chains of thought —the scratchpads they use to plan ahead and note down partial results
In theory, if a watcher LLM spots signs of undesirable activity in a model’s chain of thought, it will get flagged to a human
Typically, models were monitored in this way only once they were deployed
Chen says that OpenAI has now started monitoring all its training runs as well. “We didn’t have the monitors on in training before

It wasn’t industry practice,” he says. “Now every single thing is put through monitors.” Human reviewers can then assess whether or not flagged agents are behaving as they should: “It’s all triage.” Chen says that in the last couple of months OpenAI has shifted between 5% and 10% of its vast computing resources away from training new models and toward safety work, especially monitoring
OpenAI has also fixed some of the processes within the organization itself, establishing clearer lines of communication and quicker handoffs between its research and security teams, he says

But given how hard OpenAI sells the capabilities of its technology, why weren’t these systems and procedures in place already? Why did the company not see the hacks coming? “Even just three or four months ago, when we looked at the behavior of these agents during training, the things that were happening were kind of amusing,” says Chen. “For instance, an agent might, you know, reach out to someone on Slack for help with a task.” The signs were there, but they were misread

Cute behavior—like asking someone for help—that was rewarded during training reinforced a tendency to seek out shortcuts , a type of behavior that became far more consequential down the line. “I think the big update for us was how quickly that kind of behavior can lead to an impact with a footprint as big as the Hugging Face incident,” says Chen

According to new reporting by the New York Times yesterday, OpenAI employees warned executives , including the firm’s president, Greg Brockman, months before the Hugging Face hack that its models were not being monitored properly during training.  An OpenAI spokesperson says: “As frontier models have become more capable, we continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster
We know we have more work to do, and we’ve recently slowed development and held back models that don’t meet our safety bar

We continue to make significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, and use real-time monitoring to respond faster to misaligned behavior.”  Race vs. pace OpenAI’s rivals have taken note
Spurred by the fallout from the incident, the major AI labs—including Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and SpaceXAI—have all called for the pace of development to slow down

But how does that square with fierce international competition and trillion-dollar IPOs? “We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot and take ourselves far off the frontier—that’s just a horrible strategy,” he says. “I think it’s really about setting a norm
The more that we can set that norm, it’ll be safer for the industry as a whole.” Coordination across US companies will be hard enough
Establishing global norms is harder still, especially given concerns around AI’s impact on national security

title: What Democrats are still getting wrong about voters
excerpt: Congressional Democrats outside the US Capitol on May 21, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images With the 2026 midterm elections fast approaching, po
body: Congressional Democrats outside the US Capitol on May 21, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images With the 2026 midterm elections fast approaching, polling increasingly suggests that the GOP is in for a bad time

As the Iran war drives up inflation and fuel prices , Republicans are on the back foot not just in swing states like Michigan, but in redder parts of the map: Iowa, Texas, and maybe even Kansas , among others. (Not to mention Georgia and North Carolina .)  It’s shaping up to be a Democratic wave, in other words, and a major repudiation of President Donald Trump

According to Sarah Longwell, the publisher of political news site the Bulwark, there’s a clear reason why this is the cycle that things seem to be falling apart for Trump, who has dodged scandals and bad poll numbers before. “The average person is often voting on instinctual things,” she explains, “and those instincts are a lot of your animalistic desires for things to be okay materially.” And for many voters right now, things are not okay materially

Longwell would know: She regularly speaks with voters for her podcast, The Focus Group , and she’s the author of the new book How to Eat an Elephant: One Voter at a Time .  Longwell talked with Vox’s Astead Herndon for a special live recording of the America, Actually podcast at the Texas Tribune Festival earlier this month about why voters are both more and less complicated than punditry sometimes suggests, what the future holds for the Republican Party post-Trump, and the lesson Democrats need to learn to capitalize on their wins
Below is an excerpt of Astead’s conversation with Longwell, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
One of the themes in the book is to talk to voters like real adults
What does that mean?  There was a long period of time in our history where the artifice of politics was part of the performance of politics
Those are not the rules of politics in this communications environment anymore
Every single one of you, if you’re a Bulwark person, you interact with me
I am in your ear, and we’re having a conversation
I walked in here and met a bunch of people, and they were like, “I feel like I know you.” And people want to feel like that about their political leaders now
And so they want to know what makes you tick
Are you a real person? And so the artifice of a debate on CNN is starting to feel really stupid, no offense to CNN
And a lot of it is just that artifice is falling away for voters
Donald Trump understood that as a person who had been in people’s living rooms as a performer

Democratic politicians still have not figured it out.  One of the things that comes through in both the book and I think the work that we both do is how voters don’t always fit into those neat ideological boxes

I always tell the story about when I was at the Iowa caucuses, and I remember in 2019 in the Democratic primary, someone telling me they were stuck between Bernie [Sanders] and [former New York City Mayor Michael] Bloomberg, and asking, “How did you get there?” And what was the answer?  I think the short answer was they liked a strong guy where they knew what he believed in
And they did not care which side of that coin that was, as long as it felt consistent and something they could put their hands around
If ideology is not the controlling paradigm for voters, how should we think about the different ways people are sorting themselves right now?  My answer is genuinely not to sort them as much

This is the reason people say things like, “It’s the economy, stupid,” and then everybody gets bored with that answer, and they want to talk about 10 other things because they’re like, “Well, that’s so straightforward.” But I try in the book to say it really is about improving people’s material well-being and ensuring their safety
So you go back to: What are the most human things that people want? They want to be able to afford gas
They want a job [where] they think that they can go up the ladder
They want their kids to get a good education
They want to know that they’re safe in their community
They want to know they’re safe in the places that they go

And Donald Trump and Republicans really do understand: People vote with weird animal instincts.  Now, I bet a lot of the people in this room are college-educated suburban voters, but the average voter in a general election is a 55-year-old white guy without a college degree

The average person is often voting on instinctual things, and those instincts are a lot of your animalistic desires for things to be okay materially — your cost of health care, and then for you to be safe

And so if you think about those base-level desires and then think about what Democrats spend most of their time talking about, you’re like, “Is that the thing that captures all these people?” When I watch Democrats as somebody who’s an immigrant into the Democratic ecosystem, there’s a lot of, like, “And you get a policy, and you get a policy, and you get a policy.” And I don’t really understand that because everybody needs cheaper gas
Everybody needs groceries that they can afford

And so talking about the things that unite us or that everybody needs, to me, is the secret sauce for how Democrats should think about policy.  Three years ago, Democrats thought that being against January 6th was a thing that united everybody
There was a belief that pro-democracy arguments were going to unite people across ideology
Why did that fail in 2024?  I’ve been thinking about this a lot as Trump gets terrible poll after terrible poll, and this is my point
The coup, all of the horrible things he said about women, all of the lawsuits — I mean, he told everybody an election was stolen
Why is he underwater right now? Because of gas prices, because of a war in Iran, because the negative personal consequences of his policies are hitting people

I’m so aware of the frustration where people are like, “Why are people so selfish? Why don’t they think about the bigger picture of democracy?” And one of the things I try not to do is magic words — consultant stuff, because a lot of consultants do that
They’re like, “Say freedom,” and “Say affordability.” There’s nothing to back it up
But the one magic word I do think that Democrats should start using is “America,” and swap it in for “democracy.” And the reason is, voters practice democracy in America by its individual things
So they like the elements of democracy, but they don’t think about them up here as democracy
And also the word democracy now is very polarized, right? Republicans think that Democrats are a threat to democracy because they stole the 2020 election

When can we say AI made a scientific discovery? Last week, Anthropic announced that its new molecular biology lab had made its first discovery: its AI agents had flagged a previously uncatalogued pattern surrounding an enzyme, a pattern “reminiscent” of what led to the gene-editing technology CRISPR
Some questioned whether merely finding the pattern amounted to a discovery at all
Another said his team had already discovered the same pattern, raising questions about whether Anthropic’s system had learned from his conversations with Claude
It’s a reminder that what’s novel for AI may be routine, unsurprising or simply not that consequential to a biologist
And the grand claims could make real progress harder to recognize

title: At least 27 dead after two mass shootings in South Africa, police say

body: Seventeen people killed near Johannesburg in suspected ‘illegal goldmining turf war’, as 10 killed in separate incident at barbecue venue near Cape Town Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, as the country grapples with one of the world’s highest murder rates amid investigations into corruption and criminality within the police

The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 assault rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, about 50 miles south-west of central Johannesburg
At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said
